In order to prove this theorem, Hall first showed the following lemma. Let $( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ be a system of sets with at least one transversal and let $R$ be the intersection of all transversals. Then there is an $I \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ with $A _ { I } = R$ and $| I | = | R |$ .

Hall proved this with the help of an alternating path argument. Having the lemma, the theorem is easy, by induction on $n$ : we may assume that $( A _ { 1 } , \dotsc , A _ { n - 1 } )$ has a transversal; let $R ^ { \prime }$ be the intersection of all these transversals. So by the lemma, $R ^ { \prime } = A _ { I ^ { \prime } }$ for some $I ^ { \prime } \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , n - 1 \}$ with $| I ^ { \prime } | = | R ^ { \prime } |$ . Hence $A _ { n } \ \nsubseteq { R ^ { \prime } }$ , since otherwise for $I : = I ^ { \prime } \cup \{ n \}$ one has $\begin{array} { r } { | \bigcup _ { i \in I } A _ { i } | = | R ^ { \prime } | < | I | } \end{array}$ . Therefore, $\left( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n - 1 } \right)$ has a transversal not containing $A _ { n }$ as a subset, implying that $( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ has a transversal.

Hall derived as a consequence that if $A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n }$ and $B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n }$ are two partitions of a finite set $S$ , then the two partitions have a common transversal if and only if for each subset $I$ of $\{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ , the set $\cup _ { i \in I } A _ { i }$ intersects at least $| I |$ sets among $B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n }$ . Hall remarked that the theorem of K˝onig [1916] on the existence of a perfect matching in a regular bipartite graph follows as an immediate corollary, and that also a theorem of Rado [1933] can be derived (the K˝onig-Rado edge cover theorem — Theorem 19.4), but he did not observe that Hall’s marriage theorem is equivalent to a theorem of K˝onig [1931] (K˝onig’s matching theorem — Theorem 16.2).

As for common transversals, Maak [1936] showed that if $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } )$ are partitions of a finite set $S$ , then $\mathcal { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ have a common transversal if and only if for each $I \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ , the set $\cup _ { i \in I } A _ { i }$ contains at most $| I |$ of the sets $B _ { i }$ as a subset. This can be derived from Frobenius’ theorem (Frobenius [1917]).

The basic characterization of common transversals of two arbitrary families of sets was given by Ford and Fulkerson [1958c] — see Section 23.1.

Shmushkovich [1939] and de Bruijn [1943] extended the results to the infinite case. Weyl [1949] introduced the name ‘marriage theorem’ for Hall’s marriage theorem. Maak [1952] gave some historical notes.

# Chapter 23

# Common transversals

We consider sets that are transversals of two families of sets simultaneously. Again we denote, for any family $( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ of sets and any $I \subseteq$ $\{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ ,

$$
A _ { I } : = \bigcup _ { i \in I } A _ { i } .
$$

# 23.1. Common transversals

Let $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ be families of sets. A set $T$ is called a common transversal of $\mathcal { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ if $T$ is a transversal of both $\mathcal { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ . Similarly, $T$ is called a common partial transversal of $\mathcal { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ if $T$ is a partial transversal of both $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { \beta }$ .

When considering two families ${ \mathcal { A } } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { m } )$ of subsets of a set $S$ , it is helpful to construct the following directed graph $D = ( V , A )$ :

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { V : = \{ a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { n } \} \cup S \cup \{ b _ { 1 } , \ldots , b _ { m } \} , } \\ & { A : = \{ ( a _ { i } , s ) \mid i = 1 , \ldots , n ; s \in A _ { i } \} \cup \{ ( s , b _ { i } ) \mid i = 1 , \ldots , m ; s \in } \\ & { B _ { i } \} , } \end{array}
$$

where $a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { n } , b _ { 1 } , \ldots , b _ { m }$ are distinct new elements, not in $S$ .

Then one has, if $m = n$ :

a subset $T$ of $S$ is a common transversal of $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ if and only if $D$ has $n$ vertex-disjoint paths from $\{ a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { n } \}$ to $\{ b _ { 1 } , \ldots , b _ { n } \}$ such that $T$ is the set of vertices in $S$ traversed by these paths.

A similar statement can be formulated with respect to common partial transversals.

With Menger’s theorem, it yields the following characterization of the existence of a common transversal, due to Ford and Fulkerson [1958c]:

Theorem 23.1. Let $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } )$ be families of sets. Then $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ have a common transversal if and only if

$$
| A _ { I } \cap B _ { J } | \geq | I | + | J | - n
$$

for all $I , J \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ .

Proof. To see necessity, let $T$ be a common transversal. To prove (23.3), we can assume that $A _ { i } \subseteq T$ and $B _ { j } \subseteq T$ for all $i , j$ . Then

$$
| A _ { I } \cap B _ { J } | = | A _ { I } | + | B _ { J } | - | A _ { I } \cup B _ { J } | \ge | I | + | J | - | T | \ge | I | + | J | - n
$$

for all $I , J \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ .

To see sufficiency, make the digraph $D$ associated to $A , B$ as in (23.1). Let $U : = \{ a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { n } \}$ and $W : = \{ b _ { 1 } , \ldots , b _ { n } \}$ . Then by (23.2), $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ have a common transversal if $D$ has $n$ disjoint $U - W$ paths. By Menger’s theorem, these paths exist if $| C | \geq n$ for each $C \subseteq U \cup S \cup W$ intersecting each $U - W$ path. To check this condition, let $I : = \{ i \mid a _ { i } \notin C \}$ and $J : = \{ j \ | \ b _ { j } \ \notin C \}$ . Then

$$
C \cap S \supseteq A _ { I } \cap B _ { J } ,
$$

since $A _ { I } \cap B _ { J }$ is equal to the set of vertices in $S$ that are on a $U - W$ path not intersected by $C \cap ( U \cup W )$ . So (23.3) implies

$$
| C \cap S | \geq | A _ { I } \cap B _ { J } | \geq | I | + | J | - n = ( n - | C \cap U | ) + ( n - | C \cap W | ) - n ,
$$

giving $| C | \geq n$ .

(For a direct derivation of this theorem from Hall’s marriage theorem, see Perfect [1969c]. For a derivation from the K˝onig-Rado edge cover theorem, see Perfect [1980].)

This construction also implies, with Theorem 9.8, that a common transversal of two collections of $n$ subsets of $S$ can be found in time $O ( n ^ { 3 / 2 } | S | )$ (cf. Adel’son-Vel’ski˘ı, Dinits, and Karzanov [1975]).

Perfect [1968] (cf. McDiarmid [1973]) strengthened Theorem 23.1 to a min-max relation for the maximum size of a common partial transversal:

Corollary 23.1a. Let $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { m } )$ be families of sets and let $k \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + }$ . Then $A$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ have a common partial transversal of size $k$ if and only if

$$
| A _ { I } \cap B _ { J } | \geq | I | + | J | - n - m + k
$$

for all $I \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ and $J \subseteq \{ 1 , \dots , m \}$ .

Proof. We may assume that $m = n$ (if, say, $n < m$ , add $m - n$ copies of $\varnothing$ to $\boldsymbol { A }$ ). Let $X$ be a set disjoint from all $A _ { i }$ and $B _ { i }$ with $| X | = n - k$ . Replace each $A _ { i }$ by $A _ { i } ^ { \prime } : = A _ { i } \cup X$ and each $B _ { i }$ by $B _ { i } ^ { \prime } : = B _ { i } \cup X$ . Then $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ have a common partial transversal of size $k$ if and only if $\mathcal { A } ^ { \prime } = ( A _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , \ldots , A _ { n } ^ { \prime } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B ^ { \prime } } = ( B _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , \ldots , B _ { n } ^ { \prime } )$ have a common transversal. Applying Theorem 23.1 to $\mathcal { A } ^ { \prime }$ and $B ^ { \prime }$ gives this corollary. I

Generally, a common partial transversal of families $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ need not be contained in a common transversal, even not if a common transversal exists:

let $\mathcal { A } : = ( \{ a \} , \{ b , c \} )$ and $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { B } } : = ( \{ b \} , \{ a , c \} )$ . Then $\{ c \}$ is a common partial transversal, while $\{ a , b \}$ is the only common transversal.

The following result of Perfect [1968] and Welsh [1968] characterizes subsets contained in common transversals. It is a special case of a theorem of Ford and Fulkerson [1958c] (cf. Theorem 23.14), and will be derived from Theorem 23.1 with a method of Mirsky and Perfect [1968].

Corollary 23.1b. Let $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } )$ be families of subsets of a set $S$ and let $X \subseteq S$ . Then $\mathcal { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { \beta }$ have a common transversal containing $X$ if and only if

$$
| A _ { I } \cap B _ { J } | \geq | I | + | J | - n + | X \setminus ( A _ { I } \cup B _ { J } ) |
$$

for all $I , J \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ .

Proof. To see necessity, we can assume that there is a common transversal $T$ containing each $A _ { i }$ , each $B _ { j }$ , and $X$ . Then for all $I , J \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ :

$$
| A _ { I } \cap B _ { J } | = | A _ { I } | + | B _ { J } | - | A _ { I } \cup B _ { J } | \geq | I | + | J | + | X \setminus ( A _ { I } \cup B _ { J } ) | - n
$$

since $| A _ { I } \cup B _ { J } | + | X \setminus ( A _ { I } \cup B _ { J } ) | \leq | T | = n$ .

To see sufficiency, let $X = \{ x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { k } \}$ and let $x _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , \ldots , x _ { k } ^ { \prime }$ be new elements. For each $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ , let $A _ { i } ^ { \prime }$ be the set obtained from $A _ { i }$ by replacing any occurrence of $x _ { j }$ by $\boldsymbol { x } _ { j } ^ { \prime }$ . Then $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ have a common transversal containing $X$ if the families

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \mathcal { A } ^ { \prime } : = ( A _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , \dotsc , A _ { n } ^ { \prime } , \{ x _ { 1 } \} , \dotsc , \{ x _ { k } \} ) \mathrm { ~ a n d } } \\ & { \mathcal { B } ^ { \prime } : = ( B _ { 1 } , \dotsc , B _ { n } , \{ x _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } \} , \dotsc , \{ x _ { k } ^ { \prime } \} ) } \end{array}
$$

have a common transversal. So by Theorem 23.1 we must check condition (23.3) for $\mathcal { A } ^ { \prime }$ and $B ^ { \prime }$ . Let $I , J \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ and $I ^ { \prime } , J ^ { \prime } \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , k \}$ . Define $Y : = \{ x _ { i } \mid i \in I ^ { \prime } \}$ and $Z : = \{ x _ { i } \mid i \in J ^ { \prime } \}$ . Then

$$
\begin{array}{c} { \begin{array} { r l } & { { \big | } { \bigl ( } \bigcup A _ { i } ^ { \prime } \cup \bigcup \bigcup \bigcup \left\{ x _ { i } \right\} { \big ) } \cap { \bigl ( } \bigcup B _ { j } \cup \bigcup \bigcup _ { j \in J ^ { \prime } } \ X _ { j } ^ { \prime } { \bigr \} { \bigr ) } { \big | } } \\ & { { \begin{array} { r l } & { { \mathrm { ~ } } j \in I } \\ { = { \big | } \left( A _ { I } \cap B _ { J } \right) \setminus X { \big | } + { \big | } A _ { I } \cap Z { \big | } + { \big | } B _ { J } \cap Y { \big | } } \end{array} } } \\ & { = { \big | } { \bigl ( } A _ { I } \cap B _ { J } { \bigr ) } \setminus X { \big | } + { \big | } Z { \big | } - { \big | } Z \setminus A _ { I } { \big | } + { \big | } Y { \big | } - { \big | } Y \setminus B _ { J } { \big | } } \\ & { \geq { \big | } { \bigl ( } A _ { I } \cap B _ { J } { \big ) } \setminus X { \big | } + { \big | } Z { \big | } - { \big | } X \setminus A _ { I } { \big | } + { \big | } Y { \big | } - { \big | } X \setminus B _ { J } { \big | } } \\ & { = { \big | } A _ { I } \cap B _ { J } { \big | } - { \big | } X \setminus { \big ( } A _ { I } \cup B _ { J } { \big ) } { \big | } + { \big | } Y { \big | } + { \big | } Z { \big | } - { \big | } X { \big | } } \\ & { \geq { \big | } I { \big | } + { \big | } J { \big | } + { \big | } Y { \big | } + { \big | } Z { \big | } - { \big | } X { \big | } - n = { \big | } I { \big | } + { \big | } I ^ { \prime } { \big | } + { \big | } J { \big | } + { \big | } J ^ { \prime } { \big | } - n - k } \end{array} } } \end{array} 
$$

(the last inequality follows from (23.8)).

# 23.2. Weighted common transversals

Consider the problem of finding a minimum-weight common transversal: given families ${ \mathcal { A } } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $B = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } )$ of subsets of a set $S$ and a weight function $w : S  \mathbb { Q }$ , find a common transversal $T$ of $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ minimizing $w ( T )$ . This problem can easily be solved by solving an associated minimum-cost flow problem.

Alternatively, it can be solved with the Hungarian method, as follows. For $s \in S$ , introduce a copy $s ^ { \prime }$ of $s$ . Let $S ^ { \prime } : = \{ s ^ { \prime } \mid s \in S \}$ . Let $a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { n } , b _ { 1 } , \ldots , b _ { n }$ be vertices. Make a bipartite graph $G$ with colour classes $\{ a _ { 1 } , \dots , a _ { n } \} \cup S$ and $\{ b _ { 1 } , \ldots , b _ { n } \} \cup S ^ { \prime }$ . Vertex $a _ { i }$ is connected with vertex $s ^ { \prime } \in S ^ { \prime }$ if $s \in A _ { i }$ . Vertex $b _ { i }$ is connected with vertex $s \in S$ if $s \in B _ { i }$ . Moreover, each $s \in S$ is connected with its copy $s ^ { \prime } \in S ^ { \prime }$ . This describes all edges of $G$ .

For any perfect matching $M$ in $G$ , the set of $s \in S$ with $\{ s , s ^ { \prime } \} \not \in M$ is a common transversal of $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ . Conversely, each common transversal can be obtained in this way from a perfect matching in $G$ .

Therefore, a minimum-weight common transversal of $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ can be found by determining a maximum-weight perfect matching in $G$ , taking weight $w ( s )$ on any edge $\{ s , s ^ { \prime } \}$ and weight $0$ on any other edge of $G$ . So by Theorem 17.3 we can find a minimum-weight common transversal in time $O ( k ( m + k \log k ) )$ ), where

$$
k : = n + | S | { \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } } m : = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } ( | A _ { i } | + | B _ { i } | ) .
$$

Due to the special structure of $G$ and its weight function one can sharpen this to:

Theorem 23.2. A minimum-weight common transversal can be found in time $O ( n ( m + k \log k ) )$ , with $m$ and $k$ as in (23.12).

Proof. We may assume that $w ( s ) \geq 0$ for each $s \in S$ (we can add a constant to all weights). Then we can start the Hungarian method with the matching $M$ consisting of all edges $\{ s , s ^ { \prime } \}$ with $s \in S$ . This matching is extreme (that is, has maximum weight among all matchings of size $| M |$ ), and the Hungarian method requires only $n$ iterations to obtain a maximum-weight perfect matching. I

Note that, unlike what happened in finding a minimum-weight transversal for one family of sets, in the algorithm above we do not grow a common partial transversal — we do backtrack.

We can also obtain a min-max relation for the minimum weight of a common transversal:

Theorem 23.3. Let $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } )$ be families of subsets of a set $S$ and let $w : S  \mathbb { Z }$ be a weight function. Then the minimum weight of a common transversal of $\mathcal { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ is equal to the maximum value of

$$
\sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } ( \operatorname* { m i n } _ { s \in A _ { i } } w _ { 1 } ( s ) + \operatorname* { m i n } _ { s \in B _ { i } } w _ { 2 } ( s ) ) + ( w ( S ) - w _ { 1 } ( S ) - w _ { 2 } ( S ) )
$$

taken over $w _ { 1 } , w _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { Z } ^ { S }$ satisfying $w _ { 1 } + w _ { 2 } \geq w$

Proof. Consider the graph $G$ above. By Theorem 17.5 (or by total unimodularity), the maximum weight of a perfect matching in $G$ is equal to the minimum value of

$$
\sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } ( \lambda _ { i } + \mu _ { i } ) + \sum _ { s \in S } ( w _ { 1 } ( s ) + w _ { 2 } ( s ) )
$$

taken over $\lambda , \mu \in \mathbb { Z } ^ { n }$ and $w _ { 1 } , w _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { Z } ^ { S }$ satisfying

$$
\begin{array} { l l } { { \lambda _ { i } + w _ { 1 } ( s ) \geq 0 ~ } } & { { \mathrm { f o r ~ } i = 1 , \ldots , n ~ \mathrm { a n d ~ } s \in A _ { i } , } } \\ { { w _ { 1 } ( s ) + w _ { 2 } ( s ) \geq w ( s ) ~ } } & { { \mathrm { f o r ~ } s \in S , } } \\ { { \mu _ { i } + w _ { 2 } ( s ) \geq 0 ~ } } & { { \mathrm { f o r ~ } i = 1 , \ldots , n ~ \mathrm { a n d ~ } s \in B _ { i } . } } \end{array}
$$

We can assume that $\lambda _ { i } = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ - w _ { 1 } ( s ) \mid s \in A _ { i } \}$ and $\mu _ { i } = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ - w _ { 2 } ( s ) \mid s \in$ $B _ { i } \}$ for each $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ .

Now the minimum weight of a common transversal is equal to $w ( S )$ minus the maximum weight of a perfect matching in $G$ . So it is equal to the maximum value of

$$
w ( S ) - \sum _ { s \in S } ( w _ { 1 } ( s ) + w _ { 2 } ( s ) ) + \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } ( \operatorname* { m i n } _ { s \in A _ { i } } w _ { 1 } ( s ) + \operatorname* { m i n } _ { s \in B _ { i } } w _ { 2 } ( s ) ) ,
$$

where $w _ { 1 } , w _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { Z } ^ { S }$ satisfy $w _ { 1 } + w _ { 2 } \geq w$ . This is equal to (23.13).

# 23.3. Weighted common partial transversals

A maximum-weight common partial transversal can be found with the Hungarian method, like described at the beginning of Section 23.2. At any stage of the Hungarian method the current matching $M$ is extreme (that is, it has optimum weight among all matchings of size $\vert M \vert$ ). So we can also apply it (like in Theorem 23.2) to find a maximum-weight common partial transversal of two families $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { k } )$ and $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { B } } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { l } )$ of subsets of a set $S$ . Taking

$$
n : = k + l + | S | { \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } } m : = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } | A _ { i } | + \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { l } | B _ { i } | ,
$$

we have:

Theorem 23.4. A maximum-weight common partial transversal can be found in time $O ( \operatorname* { m i n } \{ k , l \} ( m + n \log n ) )$ ).

Proof. As above.

Note that, even if all weights are positive, a maximum-weight common partial transversal need not be a common transversal (a statement that is true if we delete ‘common’). To see this, let $\mathcal { A } = ( \{ a \} , \{ b , c \} )$ , $\boldsymbol { B } = ( \{ b \} , \{ a , c \} )$ , and $w ( a ) = w ( b ) = 1$ , $w ( c ) = 3$ . Then $\{ c \}$ is the only maximum-weight common partial transversal, while $\{ a , b \}$ is the only common transversal.

A min-max relation for the maximum weight of a common partial transversal can be derived from a min-max relation for the maximum weight of a matching in a bipartite graph, or from linear programming duality using total unimodularity, as we do in the proof below:

Theorem 23.5. Let $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { A } } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { k } )$ and $\boldsymbol { \mathsf { B } } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { l } )$ be families of subsets of a set $S$ and let $w : S \to \mathbb { Z } _ { + }$ be a weight function. Then the maximum weight of a common partial transversal of $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ is equal to the minimum value of

$$
\sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \operatorname* { m a x } _ { s \in A _ { i } } w _ { 1 } ( s ) + \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { l } \operatorname* { m a x } _ { s \in B _ { i } } w _ { 2 } ( s ) + ( w - w _ { 1 } - w _ { 2 } ) ( S )
$$

where $w _ { 1 } , w _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + } ^ { S }$ with $w _ { 1 } + w _ { 2 } \leq w$

Proof. The maximum weight of a common partial transversal is equal to the maximum of $w ^ { \mathsf { T } } x$ where $x \in \mathbb { Z } ^ { S }$ such that there exist $y _ { 1 } ( i , s ) \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + }$ ( $i = 1 , \ldots , k$ ; $s \in A _ { i }$ ) and $y _ { 2 } ( i , s ) \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + }$ ( $i = 1 , \ldots , l$ ; $s \in B _ { i }$ ) satisfying

$$
\begin{array} { r l r } {  { \sum _ { s \in A _ { i } } y _ { 1 } ( i , s ) \le 1 } } \\ & { \stackrel { s \in A _ { i } } { \sum } y _ { 2 } ( i , s ) \le 1 } & { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } i = 1 , \dots , l , } \\ & { } & \\ { \stackrel { x \in B _ { i } } { x } = \sum _ { i , s \in A _ { i } } y _ { 1 } ( i , s ) } & { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } s \in S , } \\ & { } & \\ { \quad x _ { s } = \sum _ { i , s \in B _ { i } } y _ { 2 } ( i , s ) } & { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } s \in S , } \\ & { } & \\ { \quad \quad 0 \le x _ { s } \le 1 } & { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } s \in S . } \end{array}
$$

By linear programming duality and the total unimodularity of the constraint matrix in (23.19), the maximum value is equal to the minimum value of

$$
\sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } z _ { 1 } ( i ) + \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { l } z _ { 2 } ( i ) + \sum _ { s \in S } u ( s ) ,
$$

where $z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + } ^ { k }$ and $u \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + } ^ { S }$ satisfy

$$
\begin{array} { r l r l } & { z _ { 1 } ( i ) \geq w _ { 1 } ( s ) } & { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } i = 1 , \ldots , k } \\ & { z _ { 2 } ( i ) \geq w _ { 2 } ( s ) } & { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } i = 1 , \ldots , l \mathrm { ~ } \mathrm { ~ } } \\ & { w _ { 1 } ( s ) + w _ { 2 } ( s ) + u ( s ) \geq w ( s ) } & { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } s \in S , } \end{array}
$$

for some $w _ { 1 } , w _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { Z } ^ { E }$ . We may assume that $w _ { 1 } , w _ { 2 } \ \geq \ \mathbf { 0 }$ , since replacing any negative $w _ { j } ( s )$ by $0$ does not violate (23.21). We may assume that $w _ { 1 } +$ $w _ { 2 } + u = w$ , since $w \geq \mathbf { 0 }$ , and hence we can decrease $w _ { 1 } ( s )$ , $w _ { 2 } ( s )$ or $u ( s )$ i f $w _ { 1 } ( s ) + w _ { 2 } ( s ) + u ( s ) > w ( s )$ . This gives the theorem. I

By specializing $w$ to the all-one function, Theorem 23.5 reduces to Corollary 23.1a on the maximum size of a common partial transversal. We can also derive an alternative min-max relation for the maximum weight of a common partial transversal, expressed in

$$
m ( { \mathcal { C } } , w ) : = { \mathrm { m a x i m u m ~ w e i g h t ~ o f ~ a ~ p a r t i a l ~ t r a n s v e r s a l ~ o f ~ } } { \mathcal { C } }
$$

for any family $c$ and weight function $w$ (so we can plug in a min-max relation for $m ( \mathcal { C } , w )$ to obtain a genuine min-max relation):

Corollary 23.5a. Let $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { k } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { l } )$ be families of subsets of a set $S$ and let $w : S \to \mathbb { Z } _ { + }$ be a weight function. Then the maximum weight of a common partial transversal of $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ is equal to the minimum value of $m ( \mathcal { A } , w _ { 1 } ) + m ( \mathcal { B } , w _ { 2 } )$ , taken over $w _ { 1 } , w _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + } ^ { S }$ with $w _ { 1 } + w _ { 2 } = w$ .

Proof. Clearly, the maximum value here cannot be larger than the minimum value, since $w ( T ) = w _ { 1 } ( T ) + w _ { 2 } ( T ) \leq m ( A , w _ { 1 } ) + m ( B , w _ { 2 } )$ for any maximumweight common partial transversal $T$ .

To see equality, consider $w _ { 1 }$ and $w _ { 2 }$ of Theorem 23.5, and let $w _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } : = w - w _ { 1 }$ Then for any partial transversal $T _ { 1 }$ of $\boldsymbol { A }$ one has

$$
w _ { 1 } ( T _ { 1 } ) \leq \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \operatorname* { m a x } _ { s \in A _ { i } } w _ { 1 } ( s ) .
$$

Moreover, for any partial transversal $T _ { 2 }$ of $\boldsymbol { B }$ one has

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle w _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } ( T _ { 2 } ) = w _ { 2 } ( T _ { 2 } ) + ( w - w _ { 1 } - w _ { 2 } ) ( T _ { 2 } ) } } \\ { { \le \displaystyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \operatorname* { m a x } _ { s \in B _ { i } } w _ { 2 } ( s ) + ( w - w _ { 1 } - w _ { 2 } ) ( S ) . } } \end{array}
$$

So by Theorem 23.5 we have that $m ( \mathcal { A } , w _ { 1 } ) + m ( \mathcal { B } , w _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } )$ is not more than the maximum $w$ -weight of a common partial transversal.

The obvious generalization to common partial transversals of three families is not true: take

$$
\mathcal { A } = ( \{ a \} , \{ b , c \} ) , \mathcal { B } = ( \{ b \} , \{ a , c \} ) , \mathrm { a n d }
$$

and $w ( a ) = w ( b ) = w ( c ) = 1$ . Then the maximum weight of a common partial transversal is $^ { 1 }$ , but one cannot decompose $w$ as $w = w _ { 1 } + w _ { 2 } + w _ { 3 }$ with $m ( \mathcal { A } , w _ { 1 } ) + m ( \mathcal { B } , w _ { 2 } ) + m ( \mathcal { C } , w _ { 3 } ) = 1$ .

# 23.4. The common partial transversal polytope

Let $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { k } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { l } )$ be families of subsets of a set $S$ . The common partial transversal polytope Pcommon partial transversal $( A , B )$ of

$\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ is the convex hull of the incidence vectors (in $\mathbb { R } ^ { S }$ ) of the common partial transversals of $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ . That is,

$\begin{array} { r l } & { P _ { \mathrm { c o m m o n ~ p a r t i a l ~ t r a n s v e r s a l } } ( { \cal A } , { \mathcal B } ) = \mathrm { c o n v . h u l l } \{ \chi ^ { T } \mid T } \\ & { \mathrm { p a r t i a l ~ t r a n s v e r s a l ~ o f ~ } \mathcal { A } \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } { \mathcal { B } } \} . } \end{array}$ is a common

It is easy to see that each vector $x$ in the common partial transversal polytope satisfies:

$$
\begin{array} { r l r } & { 0 \le x _ { s } \le 1 } & { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } s \in S , } \\ & { x ( S \setminus A _ { I } ) \le k - | I | } & { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } I \subseteq \{ 1 , \dots , k \} , } \\ & { x ( S \setminus B _ { I } ) \le l - | I | } & { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } I \subseteq \{ 1 , \dots , l \} . } \end{array}
$$

In fact, this fully determines the common partial transversal polytope:

Theorem 23.6. The common partial transversal polytope is determined by (23.27).

Proof. We must show that for any weight function $w \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + } ^ { S }$ , the maximum value of $w ^ { 1 } x$ over (23.27) is equal to the maximum weight $\mu$ of any common partial transversal. By Corollary 23.5a, there exist weight functions $w _ { 1 } , w _ { 2 } \in$ $\mathbb { Z } ^ { S }$ with $w = w _ { 1 } + w _ { 2 }$ and $\mu = m ( A , w _ { 1 } ) + m ( B , w _ { 2 } )$ . Now any $x$ satisfying $( 2 3 . 2 7 )$ belongs to the partial transversal polytopes of $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ . So $w _ { 1 } ^ { \mathsf { T } } x \leq$ $m ( \mathcal { A } , w _ { 1 } )$ and $w _ { 2 } ^ { 1 } x \le m ( B , w _ { 2 } )$ . Hence $w ^ { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { I } } } \boldsymbol { x } \le \mu$ . I

Since (23.27) is the union of the systems that determine the partial transversal polytope of $\boldsymbol { A }$ and of $\boldsymbol { B }$ , we have:

Corollary 23.6a. Let $\mathcal { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { \beta }$ be families of subsets of a set $S$ . Then

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { P _ { \mathrm { c o m m o n ~ p a r t i a l ~ t r a n s v e r s a l } } ( \mathcal { A } , \mathcal { B } ) } \\ & { = P _ { \mathrm { p a r t i a l ~ t r a n s v e r s a l } } ( \mathcal { A } ) \cap P _ { \mathrm { p a r t i a l ~ t r a n s v e r s a l } } ( \mathcal { B } ) . } \end{array}
$$

Proof. Directly from Theorem 23.6 and Corollary 22.9a.

Also:

Theorem 23.7. System (23.27) is TDI.

Proof. Directly from Corollaries 23.5a and 22.9a.

Again one cannot make the obvious extension to three families of sets, by considering the families (23.25). In that case, the vector $\bigl ( \frac { 1 } { 2 } , \frac { 1 } { 2 } , \frac { 1 } { 2 } \bigr )$ belongs to the intersection of the three partial transversal polytopes, but does not belong to the common partial transversal polytope.

# 23.5. The common transversal polytope

Similar results hold for the common transversal polytope. Let $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \dotsc $ , $A _ { n }$ ) and $B = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } )$ be families of subsets of a set $S$ . The common transversal polytope $P _ { \mathrm { c o m m o n ~ t r a n s v e r s a l } } ( A )$ of $\mathcal { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ is the convex hull of the incidence vectors (in $\mathbb { R } ^ { S }$ ) of the common transversals of $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { \beta }$ . That is,

$\begin{array} { r l } & { P _ { \mathrm { c o m m o n ~ t r a n s v e r s a l } } ( \mathcal { A } , \mathcal { B } ) = \mathrm { c o n v . h u l l } \{ \chi ^ { T } ~ \vert ~ T } \\ & { \mathrm { v e r s a l ~ o f ~ } \mathcal { A } \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } \mathcal { B } \} . } \end{array}$ is a common trans

It is easy to see that each vector $x$ in the common transversal polytope satisfies:

$$
\begin{array} { r l r } & { 0 \leq x _ { s } \leq 1 } & { \mathrm { f o r ~ } s \in S , } \\ & { x ( A _ { I } ) \geq | I | } & { \mathrm { f o r ~ } I \subseteq \{ 1 , \dots , n \} , } \\ & { x ( B _ { I } ) \geq | I | } & { \mathrm { f o r ~ } I \subseteq \{ 1 , \dots , n \} , } \\ & { x ( S ) = n . } \end{array}
$$

Corollary 23.7a. The common transversal polytope is determined by (23.30).

Proof. The common transversal polytope is the facet of the common partial transversal polytope determined by the equality $x ( S ) = n$ . So we must show that $( 2 3 . 3 0 )$ implies (23.27), which is trivial, since if $x$ satisfies (23.30), then $x ( S \setminus A _ { I } ) = x ( S ) - x ( A _ { I } ) \leq n - | I |$ and $x ( S \setminus B _ { I } ) = x ( S ) - x ( B _ { I } ) \leq n - | I |$ for any $I \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ .

Again this implies:

Corollary 23.7b. Let $\mathcal { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ be families of subsets of a set $S$ . Then

$$
P _ { \mathrm { c o m m o n ~ t r a n s v e r s a l } } ( { \cal A } , { \cal B } ) = P _ { \mathrm { t r a n s v e r s a l } } ( { \cal A } ) \cap P _ { \mathrm { t r a n s v e r s a l } } ( { \cal B } ) .
$$

Proof. Directly from Corollaries 23.7a and 22.9b.

In fact:

Theorem 23.8. System (23.30) is TDI.

Proof. This follows from Theorem 23.7, using Theorem 5.25.

Weinberger [1976] proved the following conjecture of Fulkerson [1971a], which generalizes Theorem 18.8. Let $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } )$ be families of subsets of a set $S$ . Then the up hull P ↑common transversal(A, B) of the common transversal polytope is determined by:

$x ( U ) \geq n -$ maximum size of a common partial transversal contained in $S \setminus U$ ,

for $U \subseteq S$ . This will follow from Theorem 46.3 on polymatroids.

# 23.6. Packing and covering of common transversals

Fulkerson [1971b] and de Sousa [1971] detected that results on bipartite edgecolouring (or related results) imply characterizations of packings of common transversals. It was noticed by Brualdi [1971b] that the methods in fact yield more general results.

Basic is the following exchange property given by de Sousa [1971]:

Theorem 23.9. Let $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { m } )$ be families of subsets of a set $S$ and let $k \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + }$ . Suppose that $S$ can be covered by $k$ partial transversals of $\boldsymbol { A }$ and that $S$ can also be covered by $k$ partial transversals of $\boldsymbol { B }$ . Then $S$ can be covered by $k$ common partial transversals of $\mathcal { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ .

Proof. Let $T _ { 1 } , \dots , T _ { k }$ be a partition of $S$ into $k$ partial transversals of $\boldsymbol { A }$ . Since each $T _ { i }$ is a partial transversal of $\boldsymbol { A }$ , it follows that each $A _ { i }$ has a subset $A _ { i } ^ { \prime }$ such that $| A _ { i } ^ { \prime } | \leq k$ and such that $A _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , \ldots , A _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ partition $S$ . We can assume that $A _ { i } ^ { \prime } = A _ { i }$ for each $i$ , and hence that $\boldsymbol { A }$ is a partition of $S$ into classes of size at most $k$ .

Similarly, we can assume that $\boldsymbol { B }$ is a partition of $S$ into classes of size at most $k$ .

Now make a bipartite graph $G$ , with colour classes $\{ a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { n } \}$ and $\{ b _ { 1 } , \ldots , b _ { m } \}$ , connecting $a _ { i }$ and $b _ { j }$ by $| A _ { i } \cap B _ { j } |$ parallel edges. So $G$ has maximum degree $k$ , and hence, by K˝onig’s edge-colouring theorem, the edges of $G$ can be coloured with $k$ colours. It implies that $S$ can be partitioned as required. I

A consequence is a min-max formula for the minimum number of common partial transversals needed to cover $S$ , stated by Brualdi [1971b]:

Corollary 23.9a. Let $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } )$ be families of subsets of a set $S$ , each with union $S$ . Then the minimum number of common partial transversals of $\mathcal { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { \beta }$ needed to cover $S$ is equal to

$$
\Big [ \operatorname* { m a x } _ { X \ \subseteq \ S } \operatorname* { m a x } \{ \frac { | X | } { | \{ i | A _ { i } \cap X \neq \emptyset \} | } , \frac { | X | } { | \{ i | B _ { i } \cap X \neq \emptyset \} | } \} \Big ] .
$$

Proof. From Theorem 23.9, using Theorem 22.12.

Theorem 23.9 also gives a variant of the exchange property (de Sousa [1971]):

Corollary 23.9b. Let ${ \mathcal { A } } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } )$ be families of subsets of a set $S$ and let $k \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + }$ . Suppose that $S$ can be partitioned into $k$ transversals of $\mathcal { A }$ , and also can be partitioned into $k$ transversals of $\boldsymbol { \beta }$ . Then $S$ can be partitioned into $k$ common transversals of $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { \beta }$ .

Proof. Directly from Theorem 23.9, since $| S | = n k$ .

This implies another variant (de Sousa [1971]):

Corollary 23.9c. Let $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } )$ be families of subsets of a set $S$ and let $k \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + }$ . Suppose that $S$ has a partition $( S _ { 1 } , \ldots , S _ { n } )$ with $| S _ { i } | = k$ and $S _ { i } \subseteq A _ { i }$ for $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ . Suppose moreover that $S$ has $a$ partition $( Z _ { 1 } , \ldots , Z _ { n } )$ with $| Z _ { i } | = k$ and $Z _ { i } \subseteq B _ { i }$ for $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ . Then $S$ can be partitioned into common transversals of $\mathcal { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ .

Proof. Note that if $S$ has a partition $( S _ { 1 } , \ldots , S _ { n } )$ with $| S _ { i } | = k$ and $S _ { i } \subseteq A _ { i }$ for $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ , then $S$ can be partitioned into $k$ transversals of $\boldsymbol { A }$ . Similarly for $\boldsymbol { B }$ . So the present corollary follows from Corollary 23.9b. I

This gives the following basic min-max relation for the maximum number of disjoint common transversals, given by Fulkerson [1971b] and de Sousa [1971]:

Corollary 23.9d. Let ${ \mathcal { A } } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } )$ be families of sets and let $k$ be a natural number. Then $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ have $k$ disjoint common transversals if and only if

$$
| A _ { I } \cap B _ { J } | \geq k ( | I | + | J | - n ) .
$$

for all $I , J \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ .

Proof. Necessity of (23.34) being easy, we show sufficiency.

Let $\mathcal { A } ^ { \prime }$ arise by taking $k$ copies of $\boldsymbol { A }$ and let $B ^ { \prime }$ arise from taking $k$ copies of $\boldsymbol { B }$ . Condition (23.34) implies that $\mathcal { A } ^ { \prime }$ and $B ^ { \prime }$ have a common transversal, $S$ say (by Theorem 23.1). Then we can partition $S$ into subsets $A _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , \ldots , A _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ , with $A _ { i } ^ { \prime } \subseteq A _ { i }$ and $| A _ { i } ^ { \prime } | = k$ . Similarly, we can partition $S$ into subsets $B _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , \ldots , B _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ , with $B _ { i } ^ { \prime } \subseteq B _ { i }$ and $| B _ { i } ^ { \prime } | = k$ . Then by Corollary 23.9c, $S$ has a partition into $k$ common transversals of $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ . (Note that if $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ are partitions of a set, this corollary reduces to Corollary 20.9a.)

The following open problem, dealing with packing common transversals, was mentioned by Fulkerson [1971b]: Let $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { \beta }$ be families of subsets of a set $S$ and let $c \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + } ^ { S }$ . What is the maximum number $k$ of common transversals $T _ { 1 } , \dots , T _ { k }$ such that

$$
\chi ^ { T _ { 1 } } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \chi ^ { T _ { k } } \leq c ?
$$

More generally than Corollary 23.9d, one has for disjoint common partial transversals of prescribed size (Fulkerson [1971b]):

Theorem 23.10. Let $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { m } )$ be families of sets and let $k , p \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + }$ . Then there exist $k$ disjoint common partial transversals of size $p$ if and only if

$$
| A _ { I } \cap B _ { J } | \geq k ( | I | + | J | + p - n - m )
$$

for all $I \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ and $J \subseteq \{ 1 , \dots , m \}$ .

Proof. Construct $\mathcal { A } ^ { \prime }$ and $B ^ { \prime }$ as in Corollary 23.9d. By Corollary 23.1a, (23.36) implies that $\mathcal { A } ^ { \prime }$ and $B ^ { \prime }$ have a common partial transversal, $T$ say, of size $p k$ . Then each $A _ { i }$ has a subset $A _ { i } ^ { \prime }$ such that $| A _ { i } ^ { \prime } | \le k$ and such that $A _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , \ldots , A _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ partition $T$ . We can assume that $A _ { i } ^ { \prime } = A _ { i }$ for each $i$ , and hence that $\boldsymbol { A }$ is a partition of $T$ into classes of size at most $k$ .

Similarly, we can assume that $\boldsymbol { B }$ is a partition of $T$ into classes of size at most $k$ .

Now make a bipartite graph $G$ , with colour classes $\{ a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { n } \}$ and $\{ b _ { 1 } , \ldots , b _ { m } \}$ , connecting $a _ { i }$ and $b _ { j }$ by $| A _ { i } \cap B _ { j } |$ parallel edges. So $G$ has $k p$ edges and maximum degree $k$ , and hence, by Theorem 20.8, the edges of $G$ can be coloured with $k$ colours, each of size $p$ . It implies that $T$ can be partitioned into common partial transversals of $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ of size $p$ . I

Similarly to Theorem 23.9 one can prove the following exchange property:

Theorem 23.11. Let $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } )$ be families of subsets of a set $S$ and let $k \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + }$ . Suppose that $\mathcal { A }$ has $k$ disjoint transversals and that also $\boldsymbol { B }$ has $k$ disjoint transversals. Then $S$ has $k$ disjoint subsets $S _ { 1 } , \ldots , S _ { k }$ such that each $S _ { i }$ contains a transversal of $\boldsymbol { A }$ and contains a transversal of $\boldsymbol { B }$ .

Proof. As $\boldsymbol { A }$ has $k$ disjoint transversals, there exist disjoint sets $A _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , \ldots , A _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ with $A _ { i } ^ { \prime } \subseteq A _ { i }$ and $| A _ { i } ^ { \prime } | = k$ for $i = 1 , \ldots , k$ . For our purposes, we can assume that $A _ { i } ^ { \prime } = A _ { i }$ . Let $Y$ be the union of the $A _ { i }$ . Similarly, we can assume that $B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n }$ have size $k$ each and partition some set $Z$ .

Again, make a bipartite graph $G$ , with colour classes $\{ a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { n } \}$ and $\{ b _ { 1 } , \ldots , b _ { n } \}$ , connecting $a _ { i }$ and $b _ { j }$ by $| A _ { i } \cap B _ { j } |$ parallel edges. Then $G$ has maximum degree at most $k$ , and hence, by K˝onig’s edge-colouring theorem (Theorem 20.1), $G$ is $k$ -edge-colourable. It gives a partition of $Y \cap Z$ into $k$ classes each intersecting any $A _ { i }$ and $B _ { i }$ in at most one element. We can extend this partition to a partition of $Y \cup Z$ into classes each intersecting any $A _ { i }$ and any $B _ { i }$ in exactly one element. This is a partition as required. I

This implies another min-max relation:

Corollary 23.11a. Let $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } )$ be families of subsets of a set $S$ . Then the maximum number $k$ for which there exist disjoint subsets $S _ { 1 } , \ldots , S _ { k }$ each containing a transversal of $\mathcal { A }$ and a transversal of $\boldsymbol { B }$ is equal to

$$
\big \lfloor _ { \varnothing \ne I \subseteq \{ 1 , \dots , n \} } \operatorname* { m i n } _ { \varnothing \nearrow I \subseteq \{ 1 , \dots , n \} } \operatorname* { m i n } \{ \frac { | A _ { I } | } { | I | } , \frac { | B _ { I } | } { | I | } \} \big \rfloor .
$$

Proof. Directly from Theorems 22.10 and 23.11.

An analogue of Corollary 23.9d for covering by common transversals is:

Theorem 23.12. Let $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } )$ be families of subsets of $S$ and let $X \subseteq S$ . Then $X$ can be covered by $k$ common transversals if and only if

$$
k | A _ { I } \cap B _ { J } | \geq k ( | I | + | J | - n ) + | X \setminus ( A _ { I } \cup B _ { J } ) |
$$

for all $I , J \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ .

Proof. To see necessity, let $T _ { 1 } , \dots , T _ { k }$ be common transversals covering $X$ and let $I , J \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ . Then

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { k | A _ { I } \cap B _ { J } | \ge \displaystyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { k } | A _ { I } \cap B _ { J } \cap T _ { j } | } \\ & { = \displaystyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { k } ( | A _ { I } \cap T _ { j } | + | B _ { J } \cap T _ { j } | - | T _ { j } \cap ( A _ { I } \cup B _ { J } ) | ) } \\ & { \ge \displaystyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { k } ( | I | + | J | - | T _ { j } \cap ( A _ { I } \cup B _ { J } ) | ) } \\ & { = k ( | I | + | J | - n ) + \displaystyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { k } | T _ { j } \setminus ( A _ { I } \cup B _ { J } ) | } \\ & { \ge k ( | I | + | J | - n ) + | X \setminus ( A _ { I } \cup B _ { J } ) | . } \end{array}
$$

To see sufficiency, make a directed graph $D$ , with vertex set

$$
\{ r \} \cup \{ a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { n } \} \cup S \cup S ^ { \prime } \cup \{ b _ { 1 } , \ldots , b _ { n } \} ,
$$

where $S ^ { \prime }$ is a set consisting of, for each $s \in S$ , a (new) copy $s ^ { \prime }$ of $s$ , and with arcs, with demands and capacities, as follows:

$( r , a _ { i } )$ with demand $k$ and capacity $k$ , for $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ ,   
$( a _ { i } , s )$ with demand 0 and capacity $\infty$ for $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ and $s \in A _ { i }$ , $( s , s ^ { \prime } )$ with demand 1 (if $s \in X$ ) or $0$ (if $s \not \in X$ ) and capacity $k$ , for $s \in S$ ,   
$( s ^ { \prime } , b _ { i } )$ with demand 0 and capacity $\infty$ , for $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ and $s \in$ $B _ { i }$ ,   
$( b _ { i } , r )$ with demand $k$ and capacity $k$ , for $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ .

Then by Hoffman’s circulation theorem (Theorem 11.2), (23.38) implies the existence of a circulation $f$ obeying the demands and capacities. Indeed, consider any set $U$ of vertices of $D$ . Let $I : = \{ i \mid a _ { i } \in U \}$ , $J : = \{ j \mid b _ { j } \notin U \}$ , $Y : = U \cap S$ and $Z : = \{ s \in S \mid s ^ { \prime } \notin U \}$ . We can assume that the capacity of the arcs leaving $U$ is finite, and hence, if $i \in I$ , then $A _ { i } \subseteq Y$ and if $j \in J$ , then $B _ { j } \subseteq Z$ . That is, $A _ { I } \subseteq Y$ and $B _ { J } \subseteq Z$ .

If $r \not \in U$ , then the total demand of the arcs entering $U$ is equal to

$$
k | I | + | X \setminus ( Y \cup Z ) |
$$

and the total capacity of the arcs leaving $U$ is equal to

$$
k | Y \cap Z | + k ( n - | J | ) .
$$

Since $A _ { I } \subseteq Y$ and $B _ { J } \subseteq Z$ , (23.38) implies that (23.42) is at most (23.43).

If $r \in U$ , then the total demand of the arcs entering $U$ is equal to

$$
k | J | + | X \setminus ( Y \cup Z ) |
$$

and the total capacity of the arcs leaving $U$ is equal to

$$
k | Y \cap Z | + k ( n - | I | ) .
$$

Since $A _ { I } \subseteq Y$ and $B _ { J } \subseteq Z$ , (23.38) implies that (23.44) is at most (23.45).

So Hoffman’s condition is satisfied, and hence there exists a circulation $f$ .

Now $f$ is at most $k$ on any arc. Hence, by Corollary 11.2b, $f$ is the sum of $k$ $\{ 0 , 1 \}$ -valued circulations $f _ { 1 } , \ldots , f _ { k }$ . For each circulation $f _ { i }$ , the set $T _ { i }$ of $s \in S$ with $f _ { i } ( s , s ^ { \prime } ) = 1$ is a common transversal of $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ . Moreover, since $f ( s , s ^ { \prime } ) \geq 1$ for each $s \in X$ , these common transversals cover $X$ .

A covering theorem different from Theorem 23.12 is due to Brualdi [1971b]:

Theorem 23.13. Let $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { A } } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { m } )$ be families of subsets of a set $S$ . Suppose that $S$ can be covered by $k$ common partial transversals of $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { \beta }$ . Then $S$ can be covered by $k$ common partial transversals each of size $\lfloor \left| S \right| / k \rfloor$ or $\lceil \lvert S \rvert / k \rceil$ .

Proof. The assumption implies that each $A _ { i }$ contains a subset $A _ { i } ^ { \prime }$ with $| A _ { i } ^ { \prime } | \leq$ $k$ , such that the $A _ { i } ^ { \prime }$ partition $S$ . For our purposes, we can assume that $A _ { i } ^ { \prime } = A _ { i }$ for each $i$ . Similarly, we can assume that $\boldsymbol { B }$ is a partition of $S$ into classes of size at most $k$ .

Again, make a bipartite graph $G$ , with colour classes $\{ a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { n } \}$ and $\{ b _ { 1 } , \ldots , b _ { m } \}$ , connecting $a _ { i }$ and $b _ { j }$ by $| A _ { i } \cap B _ { j } |$ parallel edges. Then $G$ has maximum degree at most $k$ , and hence, by Theorem 20.8, $G$ is $k$ -edgecolourable, where each colour has size $\lfloor \left| S \right| / k \rfloor$ or $\lceil \lvert S \rvert / k \rceil$ . This yields a partition of $S$ into $k$ common partial transversals as required. I

# 23.7. Further results and notes

# 23.7a. Capacitated common transversals

Recall the definition of system of restricted representatives: Let $\mathcal { A } = \left( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } \right)$ be a collection of subsets of a set $S$ and let $a , b \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + } ^ { S }$ with $a \leq b$ . A system of restricted representatives (or $S R R$ ) of $\boldsymbol { A }$ (with respect to $a$ and $b$ ) is a sequence $\left( s _ { 1 } , \ldots , s _ { n } \right)$ such that

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \mathrm { ( i ) } \ s _ { i } \in A _ { i } \ \mathrm { f o r } \ i = 1 , \ldots , n ; } \\ & { \mathrm { ( i i ) } \ a ( s ) \leq | \{ i \mid s _ { i } = s \} | \leq b ( s ) \ \mathrm { f o r } \ s \in S . } \end{array}
$$

Ford and Fulkerson [1958c] derived the following characterization of the existence of a common system of restricted representatives from the max-flow min-cut theorem (we give the derivation from Corollary 23.1b based on splitting elements, due to Mirsky and Perfect [1968]):

Theorem 23.14. Let $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } )$ be families of subsets of a set $S$ and let $a , b \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + } ^ { S }$ with $a \leq b$ . Then $\mathcal { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ have a common system of restricted representatives if and only if

$$
b ( A _ { I } \cap B _ { J } ) \geq | I | + | J | - n + a ( S \setminus ( A _ { I } \cup B _ { J } ) )
$$

for all $I , J \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ .

Proof. Let for any $s \in S$ , $Z _ { s }$ be a set of $b ( s )$ (new) elements. Replace in each $A _ { i }$ and $B _ { j }$ , any occurrence of any $s \in S$ by the elements of $Z _ { s }$ . Choose from each $Z _ { s }$ , $a ( s )$ elements, forming the set $X$ . Then $\mathcal { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ have a common system of restricted representatives if and only if the new families have a common transversal containing $X$ . Trivially, condition (23.47) is equivalent to condition (23.8) for the new families, and hence the theorem follows from Corollary 23.1b. I

(More can be found in Mirsky [1968b].)

# 23.7b. Exchange properties

Mirsky [1968a] showed the following exchange property of common transversals:

Theorem 23.15. Let $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ and $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { m } )$ be families of sets. Let $I ^ { \prime } , I ^ { \prime \prime } \subseteq \{ 1 , . . . , n \}$ and $J ^ { \prime } , J ^ { \prime \prime } \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , m \}$ . Suppose that $( A _ { i } \ | \ i \in I ^ { \prime } )$ and $( B _ { j } \mid j \in J ^ { \prime } )$ have a common transversal, and also that $( A _ { i } \mid i \in I ^ { \prime \prime } )$ and $( B _ { j } \mid j \in$ $J ^ { \prime \prime }$ ) have a common transversal. Then there exist $I$ and $J$ with $I ^ { \prime } \subseteq I \subseteq I ^ { \prime } \cup I ^ { \prime \prime }$ and $J ^ { \prime \prime } \subseteq J \subseteq J ^ { \prime } \cup J ^ { \prime \prime }$ such that $( A _ { i } \ | \ i \in I )$ and $( B _ { j } \ | \ j \in J )$ have a common transversal.

Proof. Directly from Corollary 9.12a applied to the digraph defined in (23.1).

This implies (Mirsky [1968a]):

Corollary 23.15a. Let $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $_ { \beta }$ be families of sets and let $\mathcal { A } ^ { \prime }$ and $B ^ { \prime }$ be subfamilies of $\mathcal { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ respectively. Then there exist subfamilies $\mathcal { A } _ { 0 }$ and $B _ { 0 }$ of $\boldsymbol { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ respectively satisfying $\mathcal { A } ^ { \prime } \subseteq \mathcal { A } _ { 0 }$ and $B ^ { \prime } \subseteq B _ { 0 }$ and having a common transversal if and only if (i) $\mathcal { A } ^ { \prime }$ and some subfamily of $\boldsymbol { B }$ have a common transversal and (ii) $B ^ { \prime }$ and some subfamily of $\mathcal { A }$ have a common transversal.

Proof. Directly from Theorem 23.15.

# 23.7c. Common transversals of three families

It is NP-complete to test if three families of sets have a common transversal, even if each of the three families is a partition of $S$ (E.L. Lawler — cf. Karp [1972b]).

Theorem 23.16. Testing if three partitions have a common transversal is NPcomplete.

Proof. I. It suffices to show the NP-completeness of the following problem:

given disjoint sets $X , Y , Z$ with $| X | = | Y | \ge | Z |$ and a collection $c$ of subsets $U$ of $W : = X \cup Y \cup Z$ with $| U \cap X | = | U \cap Y | = 1$ and $| U \cap Z | \leq 1$ , decide if $c$ contains a partition of $W$ as subcollection.

To see this, first observe that we can assume that $| X | = | Y | = | Z |$ . Indeed, we can extend $Z$ by a set $R$ of size $\left| X \right| - \left| Z \right|$ and replace each doubleton $\{ x , y \}$ in $c$ by all sets $\{ x , y , w \}$ with $w \in R$ . Then the new collection contains a partition if and only if the original collection contains one.

So we can assume that $| X | = | Y | = | Z |$ . For $w \in W$ , define $\mathcal { C } _ { w } : = \{ C \in \mathcal { C } \ \in$ $\mathcal { C } \mathrm { ~ \vert ~ } w \in C \}$ . Then the collection $\{ \mathcal { C } _ { w } \ | \ w \in W \}$ is the union of three partitions of $c$ . Moreover, these three partitions have a common transversal if and only if $c$ contains a partition of $W$ . So this reduces problem (23.48) to the problem of finding a common transversal of three partitions of a set.

II. So it suffices to show the NP-completeness of (23.48). We derive this from the NP-completeness of the (more general) partition problem: decide if a given collection $\boldsymbol { B }$ of subsets of a set $Z$ contains a partition of $Z$ as a subcollection (Corollary 4.1b).

Let $V : = \{ ( B , z ) ~ | ~ z \in B \in B \}$ . Make, for each $B \in B$ , an (arbitrary) directed circuit on $\{ ( B , z ) \mid z \in B \}$ . This makes the directed graph $D$ on $V$ (consisting of vertex-disjoint directed circuits). Define $X : = V \times \{ 1 \}$ and $Y : = V \times \{ 2 \}$ . Let $c$ be the collection of

all triples $\{ ( B , z , 1 ) , ( B , z , 2 ) , z \}$ for all $B \in B$ and $z \in B$ , and all pairs $\{ ( B , z , 1 ) , ( B , z ^ { \prime } , 2 ) \}$ , for all $B \in B$ and $z , z ^ { \prime } \in B$ such that $D$ contains an arc from $z$ to $z ^ { \prime }$ .

So each element of $X \cup Y$ is in precisely two sets in $c$ : a triple and a pair. Any partition $\mathcal { P } \subseteq \mathcal { C }$ of $X \cup Y \cup Z$ contains, for any $B \in B$ , either all triples containing $B$ or all pairs containing $B$ . (Here containing $B$ means: containing $( B , z , i )$ for some $z , i$ .)

This implies that $c$ contains a partition of $X \cup Y \cup Z$ if and only if $\boldsymbol { B }$ contains a partition of $Z$ .

As indicated in this proof, the problem of finding a common transversal of three partitions is equivalent to the 3-dimensional matching problem: given a partition

$U , V , W$ of a finite set $S$ and a collection $c$ of subsets $X$ of $S$ satisfying $| X \cap U | =$ $| X \cap V | = | X \cap W | = 1$ , does $c$ have a subcollection that partitions $S$ ?

The following necessary condition for the existence of a common transversal of three families $\mathcal { A } = ( A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } )$ , $\boldsymbol { B } = ( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } )$ , and ${ \mathcal { C } } = ( C _ { 1 } , \ldots , C _ { n } )$ of sets is not sufficient: for all $I , J , K \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$

$$
\begin{array} { r } { | A _ { I } \cap B _ { J } \cap C _ { K } | \ge | I | + | J | + | K | - 2 n . } \end{array}
$$

(This would generalize condition (23.3).) To see this, consider $\mathcal { A } = ( \{ a \} , \{ b , c \} )$ , $\boldsymbol { B } = ( \{ b \} , \{ a , c \} )$ , $\mathcal { C } = ( \{ c \} , \{ a , b \} )$ .

More on common transversals of more than two families is given by Brown [1976,1984], Daci´c [1977,1979], Longyear [1977], and Zaverdinos [1981]. Woodall [1982] studied fractional transversals, and described a good characterization for the existence of a common fractional transversal for more than two families, based on linear programming.

# 23.7d. Further notes

Weinberger [1974b] observed that if the families $ { \mathcal { A } } { } = ( A _ { 1 } , . . . , A _ { n } )$ and $\begin{array} { r l } { B } & { { } = } \end{array}$ $\left( B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } \right)$ of subsets of a set $S$ are uniform (that is, all sets have the same size) and regular (that is, each $s \in S$ is in the same number of sets), then $\mathcal { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ have a common transversal.

Further work on common transversals (including extensions to the infinite case) is reported by Perfect [1969b], Brualdi [1970b,1971a], and Davies and McDiarmid [1976].

# Part III

# Nonbipartite Matching and Covering

Nonbipartite matching is a highlight of combinatorial optimization, thanks to pioneering work of Tutte and Edmonds. In particular the 1965 papers of Edmonds on nonbipartite matching opened up areas that were not accessible with the ‘classical’ methods based on flows, linear programming, and total unimodularity found in the 1950s. The papers are pioneering in polyhedral combinatorics, giving the first nontrivial characterizations of combinatorially defined polytopes.

The techniques are highly self-refining, and extend to $b$ -matchings, $b$ -factors, $T$ - joins, shortest paths in undirected graphs, and the Chinese postman problem. Nonbipartite matching also applies to practical problems where an optimal pairing has to be found, like in seat or room assignment, crew planning, and two-processor scheduling.
