\hat { f } ( U ) = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ x ( U ) \mid x \in E P _ { f } ^ { \prime } \} .
$$

Proof. By (44.34), since $E P _ { f } ^ { \prime } = E P _ { \hat { f } }$ .

${ \hat { f } } ( U )$ can be computed in strongly polynomial time:

Theorem 48.4. If a submodular set function $f$ on $S$ is given by a value giving oracle, then for each given $U \subseteq S$ , ${ \hat { f } } ( U )$ can be computed in strongly polynomial time.

Proof. We can assume that $U = S$ . Order $S = \{ s _ { 1 } , \ldots , s _ { n } \}$ arbitrarily. For $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ , define $U _ { i } : = \{ s _ { 1 } , . . . , s _ { i } \}$ . Set $x : = { \bf 0 }$ . Iteratively, for $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ , determine

$$
\mu : = \operatorname* { m i n } \{ f ( T ) - x ( T ) \mid s _ { i } \in T \subseteq U _ { i } \}
$$

(with a submodular function minimization algorithm), and reset $x ( s _ { i } ) : =$ $x ( s _ { i } ) + \mu$ .

We end up with $\boldsymbol { x } \in E P _ { f } ^ { \prime }$ and for each $u \in S$ a subset $T _ { u }$ of $S$ with $u \in T _ { u }$ and $x ( T _ { u } ) = f ( T _ { u } )$ . As the collection of subsets $T$ of $S$ with $x ( T ) = f ( T )$ i s closed under unions and intersections of intersecting sets (cf. Theorem 44.2), we can modify the $T _ { u }$ in such a way that they form a partition $U _ { 1 } , \dots , U _ { k }$ of $S$ . Then ${ \ddot { f } } ( S ) = f ( U _ { 1 } ) + \cdots + f ( U _ { k } )$ , as $x$ attains the maximum in (48.13).

As a consequence, given a submodular set function $f$ on $S$ (by a value giving oracle), we can optimize over $E P _ { f } ^ { \prime }$ in strongly polynomial time (by Corollary 44.3b, as $E P _ { f } ^ { \prime } = E P _ { \hat { f } }$ and as we can compute $\hat { f }$ ).

# 48.2a. Applications and interpretations

Graphic matroids (Dilworth [1944], also Edmonds [1970b], Dunstan [1976]). Let $G = ( V , E )$ be an undirected graph and let for each $F ^ { \prime } \subseteq E ^ { \prime }$ , $f ( F )$ be given by

$$
f ( F ) : = | \bigcup F | - 1 .
$$

It is easily checked that the function $f$ is submodular, and that the function $\hat { f }$ as given by (48.7) satisfies

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \hat { f } ( F ) = | V | \mathrm { \ m i n u s \ t h e { \ n u m b e r { \ o f } \ c o m p o n e n t s } \ o f \ t h e { \ g r a p h } \ ( \hat { V } _ { \varepsilon } } } \end{array}
$$

i.e., $\hat { f }$ is the rank function of the cycle matroid of $G$ .

Geometric interpretation. The operation of making $\hat { f }$ from $f$ can be interpreted geometrically as follows (Lov´asz [1977c], Mason [1977,1981]).

Let $\mathcal { F }$ be a collection of flats (subspaces) in a projective space, and define for each subset ${ \mathcal { F } } ^ { \prime }$ of $\mathcal { F }$ , the rank $r ( \mathcal { F } ^ { \prime } )$ by

$$
r ( \mathcal { F } ^ { \prime } ) : = \mathrm { t h e ~ } ( \mathrm { p r o j e c t i v e } ) \mathrm { d i m e n s i o n ~ o f } \bigcup \mathcal { F } ^ { \prime } .
$$

One easily checks that $r$ is nondecreasing and submodular and that $r ( \emptyset ) = 0$ . Now let

$$
f ( \mathcal { F } ^ { \prime } ) : = r ( \mathcal { F } ^ { \prime } ) - 1
$$

for ${ \mathcal { F } } ^ { \prime } \subseteq { \mathcal { F } }$ , and consider the function $\hat { f }$ . Then $\hat { f }$ can be interpreted geometrically as follows. Let $H$ be some hyperplane ‘in general position’ in the projective space. Then $\hat { f } ( \mathcal { F } ^ { \prime } )$ is equal to the projective dimension of $H \cap \cup { \mathcal { F } } ^ { \prime }$ , i.e., $\hat { f }$ is as given by (48.17) if we replace $\mathcal { F }$ by $\{ F \cap H \mid F \in { \mathcal { F } } \}$ (see Lov´asz [1977c] and Mason [1977, 1981]).

Rigidity. Let $M = ( S , { \mathcal { T } } )$ be a loopless matroid, with rank function $\boldsymbol { r }$ . Let $d$ b e a natural number. Define the set function $f$ on $S$ by

$$
f ( U ) : = d \cdot r ( U ) - d + 1 ,
$$

for $U \subseteq S$ . Again, $f$ is submodular and nondecreasing. Moreover, the function $\hat { f }$ is the rank function of a loopless matroid, as ${ \hat { f } } ( \{ s \} ) = f ( \{ s \} ) = 1$ for all $s$ in $S$ .

Let $M _ { d } = ( S , { \mathcal { T } } _ { d } )$ be this matroid. Since $E P _ { f } ^ { \prime } = E P _ { \hat { f } }$ , a subset $I$ of $S$ is independent in $M _ { d }$ if and only if

$$
| U | \leq d \cdot r ( U ) - d + 1
$$

for all $U \subseteq I$

In case $M$ is the cycle matroid of a connected graph $G = ( V , E )$ , this relates to the following (cf. Crapo [1979] and Crapo and Whiteley [1978]). Let the vertices of $G$ be placed ‘in general position’ in the $d$ -dimensional Euclidean space. Make the edges ‘rigid bars’. Suppose now that the whole graph $G$ is rigid (which only depends on $G$ and not on the embedding, since the vertices are ‘in general position’). Then $G$ is called rigid (in d dimensions). It is not difficult to see that the minimal sets $F ^ { \prime }$ of edges of $G$ for which the subgraph $( V , F )$ is rigid, form the bases of a matroid. For $d = 1$ this matroid is just the cycle matroid of $G$ , as can be checked easily. Laman [1970] (cf. Asimow and Roth [1978,1979]) showed that for $d = 2$ , a graph $G = ( V , E )$ is a base (i.e., a minimal rigid graph), if and only if

$$
{ \begin{array} { r l } & { { \mathrm { ( i ) } } \ | E | = 2 | V | - 3 , } \\ & { { \mathrm { ( i i ) } } \ | E [ U ] | \leq 2 | U | - 3 , { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ e a c h ~ } } U \subseteq V . } \end{array} }
$$

Now if $M$ is the cycle matroid of a rigid graph $G$ , with rank function $r$ , then (48.21 (ii) is equivalent to

$$
| F | \leq 2 r ( F ) - 1 , { \mathrm { f o r ~ e a c h ~ s u b s e t ~ } } F { \mathrm { ~ o f ~ } } E ,
$$

that is, by (48.20), to: $E$ is independent in the matroid $M _ { 2 }$ , as given above. Condition $( 4 8 . 2 1 ) ( \mathrm { i } )$ implies that $M _ { 2 }$ has rank $2 r ( E ) - 1$ . Hence, if $G$ is rigid in 2 dimensions, then the bases of $M _ { 2 }$ are the minimally rigid subgraphs of $G$ in 2 dimensions.

In general, the matroid of rigid subgraphs of a graph $G = ( V , E )$ (in $d$ dimensions) has rank $d | V | - { \binom { d + 1 } { 2 } } .$ . However, it is not necessarily true that $G$ is minimally rigid in $d$ dimensions if and only if $G$ has $d | V | - { \binom { d + 1 } { 2 } }$ edges and each subgraph $( U , F )$ of $G$ has at most $d | U | - { \binom { d + 1 } { 2 } }$ edges. For instance, if $G$ arises from glueing two copies of the complete graph $K _ { 5 }$ together in two vertices, and deleting the edge connecting these two vertices, then $G$ is not rigid in 3 dimensions, but it satisfies the conditions given above for $d = 3$ . (These conditions are easily seen to be necessary.)

More on the relation between rigidity and matroid union can be found in Whiteley [1988].

# 48.3. Intersection

Corollaries 48.1a and 48.1b on submodular functions $f$ not necessarily satisfying $f ( \varnothing ) \ge 0$ , can be extended to pairs of functions. Let $f _ { 1 }$ and $f _ { 2 }$ be submodular set functions on $S$ , and consider the system

$$
x ( U ) \leq f _ { i } ( U ) { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } } U \in { \mathcal { P } } ( S ) \setminus \{ \emptyset \}
$$

Then:

Theorem 48.5. System (48.23) is box-totally dual integral.

Proof. Choose $w \in \mathbb { Z } ^ { S }$ , and consider the problem dual to maximizing $w ^ { 1 } x$ over (48.23):

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \operatorname* { m i n } \{ { \displaystyle \sum _ { U \in { \mathcal P } ( S ) \backslash \{ \emptyset \} } } \left( y _ { 1 } ( U ) f _ { 1 } ( U ) + y _ { 2 } ( U ) f _ { 2 } ( U ) \right) \mid } \\ & { \qquad y _ { 1 } , y _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { \mathcal P ( S ) \backslash \{ \emptyset \} } , \displaystyle \sum _ { U \in { \mathcal P } ( S ) \backslash \{ \emptyset \} } \left( y _ { 1 } ( U ) + y _ { 2 } ( U ) \right) \chi ^ { U } = w \} . } \end{array}
$$

Let $y _ { 1 } , y _ { 2 }$ attain the minimum.

For $i \in \{ 1 , 2 \}$ , define

$$
w _ { i } : = \sum _ { U \in \mathcal { P } ( S ) \setminus \{ \emptyset \} } y _ { i } ( U ) \chi ^ { U } .
$$

By Theorem 48.1, for each $i = 1 , 2$ ,

$$
\begin{array} { r l } { \operatorname* { m i n } \{ { \displaystyle \sum _ { U \in { \mathcal P } ( S ) \backslash \{ \emptyset \} } } y _ { i } ( U ) f _ { i } ( U ) \mid } & { } \\ { y _ { i } \in { \mathbb R } _ { + } ^ { \mathcal P ( S ) \backslash \{ \emptyset \} } , \displaystyle \sum _ { U \in { \mathcal P } ( S ) \backslash \{ \emptyset \} } y _ { i } ( U ) \chi ^ { U } = w _ { i } \} } & { } \end{array}
$$

has an optimum solution $y _ { i }$ with ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { i } : = \{ U \mid y _ { i } ( U ) > 0 \}$ laminar.

These (modified) $y _ { 1 } , y _ { 2 }$ again are optimum in (48.24). As the constraints corresponding to positive components of $y _ { 1 } , y _ { 2 }$ give a totally unimodular matrix (by Theorem 41.11), Theorem 5.35 implies that system (48.23) is boxTDI. I

Theorem 48.5 implies primal integrality:

Corollary 48.5a. If $f _ { 1 }$ and $f _ { 2 }$ are submodular and integer, then $E P _ { f _ { 1 } } ^ { \prime } \cap E P _ { f _ { 2 } } ^ { \prime }$ is box-integer.

Proof. Directly from Theorem 48.5.

Given submodular functions $f _ { 1 }$ and $f _ { 2 }$ (by value giving oracles), we can as optimize over $E P _ { f _ { 1 } } ^ { \prime } = E P _ { \hat { f } _ { 1 } }$ $E P _ { f _ { 1 } } ^ { \prime } \cap E P _ { f _ { 2 } } ^ { \prime }$ f1and $E P _ { f _ { 2 } } ^ { \prime } = E P _ { \hat { f } _ { 2 } }$ in strongly polynomial time (by Corollary 47.4d, ).

# Chapter 49

# Submodularity more generally

We now discuss a number of generalizations of submodular functions, namely those defined on a subcollection $c$ of the collection of all subsets of a set $S$ . The results are similar to those for submodular functions defined on all subsets on $S$ . Often, the corresponding polyhedra form a polymatroid for some derived submodular function defined on all subsets of $S$ .

We consider three kinds of collections, in order of increasing generality: lattice families, intersecting families, and crossing families.

# 49.1. Submodular functions on a lattice family

We first consider the generalization of submodular functions to those defined on a ‘lattice family’.

Let $S$ be a finite set. A family $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ of sets is called a lattice family if

$$
T \cap U , T \cup U \in { \mathcal { C } } { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ a l l ~ } } T , U \in { \mathcal { C } } .
$$

For a lattice family $c$ , a function $f : C \to \mathbb { R }$ is called submodular if

$$
f ( T \cap U ) + f ( T \cup U ) \leq f ( T ) + f ( U )
$$

for all $T , U \in { \mathcal { C } }$ . Consider the system

$$
x ( U ) \leq f ( U ) { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } } U \in { \mathcal { C } } ,
$$

and the problem dual to maximizing $w ^ { 1 } x$ over (49.3), for $w \in \mathbb { R } ^ { S }$ :

$$
\operatorname* { m i n } \{ \sum _ { U \in \mathcal { C } } y ( U ) f ( U ) \mid y \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { \mathcal { C } } , \sum _ { U \in \mathcal { C } } y ( U ) \chi ^ { U } = w \} .
$$

Theorem 49.1. Let $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ be a lattice family, $f : C \to \mathbb { R }$ a submodular function, and $w \in \mathbb { R } ^ { S }$ . Then (49.4) has an optimum solution $y$ with ${ \mathcal { F } } : = \{ U \in { \mathcal { C } } \mid$ $y ( U ) > 0 \}$ a chain.

Proof. Let $y : C \to \mathbb { R } _ { + }$ achieve this minimum, with

$$
\sum _ { U \in { \mathcal { C } } } y ( U ) | U | | S \setminus U |
$$

as small as possible. Assume that $\mathcal { F }$ is not a chain, and choose $T , U \in { \mathcal { F } }$ with $T \nsubseteq U$ and $U \ \nsubseteq { T }$ . Let $\alpha : = \operatorname* { m i n } \{ y ( T ) , y ( U ) \}$ . Decrease $y ( T )$ and $y ( U )$ by $\alpha$ , and increase $y ( T \cap U )$ and $y ( T \cup U )$ by $\alpha$ . Since

$$
\boldsymbol { \chi } ^ { T \cap U } + \boldsymbol { \chi } ^ { T \cup U } = \boldsymbol { \chi } ^ { T } + \boldsymbol { \chi } ^ { U } ,
$$

$y$ remains a feasible solution of (49.4). As moreover

$$
f ( T \cap U ) + f ( T \cup U ) \leq f ( T ) + f ( U ) ,
$$

$f$ remains optimum. However, by Theorem 2.1, sum (49.5) decreases, contradicting our assumption.

This implies the box-total dual integrality of (49.3):

Corollary 49.1a. If $c$ is a lattice family and $f : C \to \mathbb { R }$ is submodular, then system (49.3) is box-TDI.

Proof. Consider some $w : { \mathcal { C } }  \mathbb { Z }$ , and problem (49.4) dual to maximizing $w ^ { 1 } x$ over (49.3). By Theorem 49.1, this minimum is attained by a $y$ with ${ \mathcal { F } } : = \{ U \in { \mathcal { C } } \mid y ( U ) > 0 \}$ a chain. So the constraints corresponding to positive components of $y$ form a totally unimodular matrix (by Theorem 41.11). Hence by Theorem 5.35, (49.3) is box-TDI.

For any ${ \mathcal { C } } \subseteq { \mathcal { P } } ( S )$ and $f : C \to \mathbb { R }$ , define:

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { P _ { f } : = \{ x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { S } \mid x \geq \mathbf { 0 } , x ( U ) \leq f ( U ) \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ e a c h ~ } U \in { \mathcal C } \} , } \\ & { E P _ { f } : = \{ x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { S } \mid x ( U ) \leq f ( U ) \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ e a c h ~ } U \in { \mathcal C } \} . } \end{array}
$$

Then Corollary 49.1a implies:

Corollary 49.1b. If $c$ is a lattice family and $f : C \to \mathbb { R }$ is submodular and integer, then $E P _ { f }$ is box-integer.

Proof. Directly from Corollary 49.1a.

Another consequence of Theorem 49.1 is that a submodular function $f$ on a lattice family is uniquely determined by $E P _ { f }$ (given the lattice family):

Corollary 49.1c. If $c$ is a lattice family and $f : C \to \mathbb { R }$ is submodular, then

$$
f ( U ) = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ x ( U ) \mid x \in E P _ { f } \}
$$

for each $U \in { \mathcal { C } }$

Proof. Let $w : = \chi ^ { U }$ and let $y$ attain minimum (49.4), with ${ \mathcal { F } } : = \{ T \in { \mathcal { C } }$ | $y ( T ) > 0 \}$ a chain. Since

$$
\chi ^ { U } = w = \sum _ { T \in \mathcal { F } } y ( T ) \chi ^ { T } ,
$$

we know that ${ \mathcal { F } } = \{ U \}$ and $y ( U ) = 1$ . So the maximum in (49.9) is equal to $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { T \in \mathcal { C } } y ( T ) f ( T ) = y ( U ) f ( U ) = f ( U ) } \end{array}$ . I

We note that for any lattice family ${ \mathcal { C } } \subseteq { \mathcal { P } } ( S )$ with $\cup { \mathcal { C } } = S$ , and any submodular function $f : { \mathcal { C } }  \mathbb { R }$ , the polytope $P _ { f }$ is a polymatroid. Indeed, define

$$
f ^ { \prime } ( U ) : = \operatorname* { m i n } \{ f ( T ) \mid T \in { \mathcal { C } } , T \supseteq U \} .
$$

for $U \subseteq S$ . Then $f ^ { \prime }$ is submodular, and $P _ { f ^ { \prime } } = P _ { f }$ .

# 49.2. Intersection

Also the intersection of two of the polyhedra $E P _ { f }$ is tractable. Let $S$ be a finite set. For $i = 1 , 2$ , let $\mathit { \beta } _ { \mathit { c } _ { i } }$ be a lattice family on $S$ and let $f _ { i } : C _ { i } \to \mathbb { R }$ be submodular. Consider the system

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { x ( U ) \leq f _ { 1 } ( U ) \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } U \in \mathcal { C } _ { 1 } , } \\ & { x ( U ) \leq f _ { 2 } ( U ) \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } U \in \mathcal { C } _ { 2 } . } \end{array}
$$

Then:

Corollary 49.1d. System (49.12) is box-TDI.

Proof. Choose $w \in \mathbb { R } ^ { S }$ , and consider the problem dual to maximizing $w ^ { 1 } x$ over (49.12):

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \operatorname* { m i n } \{ \displaystyle \sum _ { U \in \mathcal { C } _ { 1 } } y _ { 1 } ( U ) f _ { 1 } ( U ) + \displaystyle \sum _ { U \in \mathcal { C } _ { 2 } } y _ { 2 } ( U ) f _ { 2 } ( U ) \mid } \\ & { \qquad y _ { 1 } \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { \mathcal { C } _ { 1 } } , y _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { \mathcal { C } _ { 2 } } , \displaystyle \sum _ { U \in \mathcal { C } _ { 1 } } y _ { 1 } ( U ) \chi ^ { U } + \displaystyle \sum _ { U \in \mathcal { C } _ { 2 } } y _ { 2 } ( U ) \chi ^ { U } = w \} . } \end{array}
$$

Let $y _ { 1 } , y _ { 2 }$ attain the minimum.

For $i \in \{ 1 , 2 \}$ , define

$$
w _ { i } : = \sum _ { U \in \mathcal { C } _ { i } } y _ { i } ( U ) \chi ^ { U } .
$$

By Theorem 49.1, for each $i = 1 , 2$ ,

$$
\operatorname* { m i n } \{ \sum _ { U \in \mathcal { C } _ { i } } y _ { i } ( U ) f _ { i } ( U ) \mid y _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { \mathcal { C } _ { i } } , \sum _ { U \in \mathcal { C } _ { i } } y _ { i } ( U ) \chi ^ { U } = w _ { i } \}
$$

has an optimum solution $y _ { i }$ with ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { i } : = \{ U \in { \mathcal { C } } _ { i } \mid y _ { i } ( U ) > 0 \}$ a chain.

These $y _ { 1 } , y _ { 2 }$ again are optimum in (49.13). So, by Theorem 41.11, the constraints corresponding to positive components of $y$ form a totally unimodular matrix. Hence by Theorem 5.35, (49.12) is box-TDI.

This implies primal integrality:

Corollary 49.1e. If $f _ { 1 }$ and $f _ { 2 }$ are submodular and integer, then $E P _ { f _ { 1 } } \cap E P _ { f _ { 2 } }$ is box-integer.

Proof. Directly from Corollary 49.1d.

# 49.3. Complexity

To find the minimum of a submodular function $f$ defined on a lattice family $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ in polynomial time, just an oracle telling if a set $U$ belongs to $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ , and if so, giving $f ( U )$ , is not sufficient: if ${ \mathcal { C } } = \{ \emptyset , T , S \}$ for some $T \subseteq S$ , with $f ( \varnothing ) \ = \ f ( S ) \ = \ 0$ and $f ( T ) = - 1$ , we cannot find $T$ by a polynomially bounded number of oracle calls. So we need to have more information on $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ .

A lattice family $c$ is fully characterized by the smallest set $M$ and the largest set $L$ in $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ , together with the pre-order $\preceq$ on $S$ defined by:

$$
u \preceq v \iff \operatorname { e a c h } U \in { \mathcal { C } } \ \operatorname { c o n t a i n i n g } v \ \mathrm { a l s o \ c o n t a i n s } \ u
$$

Then $\preceq$ is a pre-order (that is, it is reflexive and transitive). A subset $U$ of $S$ belongs to $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ if and only if $M \subseteq U \subseteq L$ and $U$ is a lower ideal in $\preceq$ (that is, if $v \in U$ and $u \preceq v$ , then $u \in U$ ).

Hence $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ has a description of size $O ( | S | ^ { 2 } )$ , such that for given $U \subseteq S$ one can test in polynomial time if $U$ belongs to $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ .

For $U \subseteq S$ , define

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { U ^ { \downarrow } : = \{ s \in S \mid \exists t \in U : s \preceq t \} \mathrm { ~ a n d } } \\ & { U ^ { \uparrow } : = \{ s \in S \mid \exists t \in U : t \preceq s \} . } \end{array}
$$

Set

$$
v ^ { \uparrow } : = \{ v \} ^ { \uparrow } , v ^ { \downarrow } : = \{ v \} ^ { \downarrow } , \tilde { v } : = v ^ { \uparrow } \cap v ^ { \downarrow } .
$$

For any $U \subseteq S$ , let $\overline { U }$ be the (unique) smallest set in $c$ containing $U \cap L$ ; that is,

$$
\overline { { U } } = ( U \cap L ) ^ { \downarrow } \cup M .
$$

So having $L$ , $M$ , and $\preceq$ , the set $\bar { U }$ can be determined in polynomial time.

Determine a number $\alpha > 0$ such that

$$
\alpha \geq f ( S \setminus v ^ { \uparrow } ) - f ( ( S \setminus v ^ { \uparrow } ) \cup { \tilde { v } } ) { \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } } \alpha \geq f ( v ^ { \downarrow } ) - f ( v ^ { \downarrow } \setminus { \tilde { v } } )
$$

for all $v \in L \setminus M$ . Such an $\alpha$ can be found by at most $4 | S |$ oracle calls.

Then $\alpha$ satisfies, for any $X , Y \in { \mathcal { C } }$ with $X \subseteq Y$ :

$$
| f ( Y ) - f ( X ) | \leq \alpha | Y \setminus X | .
$$

To show this, we can assume that $Y \setminus X = \tilde { v }$ for some $v \in L \setminus M$ . Then $f ( Y ) - f ( X ) \leq f ( v ^ { \downarrow } ) - f ( v ^ { \downarrow } \setminus \tilde { v } ) \leq \alpha$ and $f ( Y ) - f ( X ) \geq f ( ( S \setminus v ^ { \uparrow } ) \cup \tilde { v } ) -$ $f ( S \setminus v ^ { \uparrow } ) \geq - \alpha$ , implying (49.21).

Now define a function ${ \bar { f } } : { \mathcal { P } } ( S ) \to \mathbb { R }$ by:

$$
\bar { f } ( U ) : = f ( \overline { { U } } ) + \alpha | \overline { { U } } \triangle U |
$$

for $U \subseteq S$ .

Then:

Theorem 49.2. For any $\alpha > 0$ satisfying (49.20) for all $v \in L \setminus M$ , the function $f$ is submodular.

Proof. First consider $T , U \subseteq L$ . Then $T \subseteq T$ and $U \subseteq { \overline { { U } } }$ , and hence:

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \bar { f } ( T ) + \bar { f } ( U ) = f ( \overline { T } ) + \alpha | \overline { T } \setminus T | + f ( \overline { U } ) + \alpha | \overline { U } \setminus U | } \\ & { \geq f ( \overline { T } \cap \overline { U } ) + \alpha | ( \overline { T } \cap \overline { U } ) \setminus ( T \cap U ) | + f ( \overline { T } \cup \overline { U } ) + \alpha | ( \overline { T } \cup \overline { U } ) \setminus ( T \cup U ) | } \\ & { \geq f ( \overline { T } \cap U ) + \alpha | \overline { T } \cap U \setminus ( T \cap U ) | + f ( \overline { T } \cup \overline { U } ) + \alpha | \overline { T } \cup U \setminus ( T \cup U ) | } \\ & { = \bar { f } ( T \cap U ) + \bar { f } ( T \cup U ) . } \end{array}
$$

(The last inequality uses (49.21), since $T \cap U \supseteq T \cap U$ (while $T \cup U = T \cup U$ ).) Hence, for $T , U \subseteq S$ one has:

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \bar { f } ( T ) + \bar { f } ( U ) = \bar { f } ( T \cap L ) + \alpha | T \setminus L | + \bar { f } ( U \cap L ) + \alpha | U \setminus L | } \\ & { \ge \bar { f } ( ( T \cap L ) \cap ( U \cap L ) ) + \bar { f } ( ( T \cap L ) \cup ( U \cap L ) ) + \alpha | T \setminus L | + \alpha | U \setminus L | } \\ & { = \bar { f } ( ( T \cap U ) \cap L ) + \bar { f } ( ( T \cup U ) \cap L ) + \alpha | ( T \cap U ) \setminus L | + \alpha | ( T \cup U ) \setminus L | } \\ & { = \bar { f } ( T \cap U ) + \bar { f } ( T \cup U ) . } \end{array}
$$

So $f$ is submodular.

The function $f$ enables us to reduce optimization problems on submodular functions defined on a lattice family, to those defined on all subsets.

Minimization. By Theorem 45.1, the minimum of $f$ can be found in strongly polynomial time. Hence

if $c$ is given by $L$ , $M$ , and $\preceq$ , and a submodular function $f :$ $c  \mathbb { R }$ is given by a value giving oracle, we can find a $U \in { \mathcal { C } }$ minimizing $f ( U )$ in strongly polynomial time.

Indeed, if $f$ attains its minimum at $U$ , then $U \in { \mathcal { C } }$ , since otherwise $\overline { { U } } \ne U$ and hence ${ \bar { f } } ( U ) > { \bar { f } } ( { \overline { { U } } } )$ (as $\alpha > 0$ ), contradicting the fact that $f$ attains its minimum at $U$ . This shows (49.25).

Maximization over $E P _ { f }$ . Given a lattice family $c$ of subsets of a set $S$ , a submodular function $f : { \mathcal { C } }  \mathbb { R }$ , and a weight function $w \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { S }$ , we can maximize $w ^ { 1 } x$ over ${ \underline { { E } } } P _ { f }$ , by adapting the greedy algorithm as follows.

Note that $\operatorname* { m a x } \{ w ^ { \mid } x \mid x \in E P _ { f } \}$ is finite if and only if $w \geq \mathbf { 0 }$ , $w ( s ) = 0$ for each $s \in S \setminus L$ , and

$$
u \preceq v { \mathrm { ~ i m p l i e s ~ } } w ( u ) \geq w ( v )
$$

for all $u , v \in S$ . If (49.26) is not the case, the maximum value is infinite, since if $u \preceq v$ , then for any $x \in E P _ { f }$ , the vector $x + \lambda ( \chi ^ { v } - \chi ^ { u } )$ belongs to $E P _ { f }$ for all $\lambda \geq 0$ . Now, if $w ( v ) > w ( u )$ , the weight increases to infinity along this line, and therefore the maximum value is $\infty$ .

So we can check in strongly polynomial time if $\operatorname* { m a x } \{ w ^ { \mathrm { ~ l ~ } } x \ \vert \ x \in E P _ { f } \}$ is finite, and therefore we can assume that it is finite. Moreover, we can assume that $L = S$ , since $w ( s ) = 0$ for each $s \in S \backslash L$ , and hence we can delete $S \backslash L$ . Similarly, we can assume that $\varnothing \in { \mathcal { C } }$ and $f ( \varnothing ) = 0$ . For if $\varnothing \in { \mathcal { C } }$ and $f ( \varnothing ) < 0$ , then $E P _ { f } = \varnothing$ , and if $f ( \varnothing ) > 0$ , we can reset $f ( \varnothing ) : = 0$ , without violating the submodularity and without modifying $E P _ { f }$ . If $\varnothing \notin { \mathcal { C } }$ , then we can add $\varnothing$ to $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ and set $f ( \varnothing ) : = 0$ , again maintaining submodularity and $E P _ { f }$ . Finally, we can assume that $\preceq$ is a partial order, since if $u \preceq v \preceq u$ , then by (49.26), $w ( u ) = w ( v )$ , and each set in $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ either contains both $u$ and $v$ , or neither of them. So we can merge $u$ and $v$ ; and in fact we can merge any set $\ddot { v }$ to one element.

Now let $\leq$ be a linear order such that for any $u , v$ , if $u \preceq v$ or $w ( u ) > w ( v )$ , then $u \leq v$ . By (49.26), the latter defines a partial order. So $\leq$ is a linear extension of it, and hence can be found in strongly polynomial time.

Let $S = \{ s _ { 1 } , \ldots , s _ { n } \}$ with $s _ { 1 } < s _ { 2 } < \cdots < s _ { n }$ . For $i = 0 , \ldots , n$ , define $U _ { i } : = \{ s _ { 1 } , . . . , s _ { i } \}$ . As $\leq$ is a linear extension of $\preceq$ , each $U _ { i }$ is a lower ideal of $\preceq$ , and hence each $U _ { i }$ belongs to $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ . Define $x ( s _ { i } ) : = f ( U _ { i } ) - f ( U _ { i - 1 } )$ for $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ . Then $x$ maximizes $w ^ { 1 } x$ over $E P _ { f }$ .

To see this, let $f$ be defined as above. Then by Theorem 44.3, $x$ belongs to $E P _ { \bar { f } }$ (as $f$ and $f$ coincide on each $U _ { i }$ ), and hence $x$ belongs to $E P _ { f }$ . To see that $x$ is optimum, we have for any $z \in E P _ { f }$ :

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { w ^ { \mathsf { T } } z = \displaystyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n - 1 } z ( U _ { i } ) ( w ( s _ { i } ) - w ( s _ { i + 1 } ) ) + z ( S ) w ( s _ { n } ) } \\ & { \le \displaystyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n - 1 } f ( U _ { i } ) ( w ( s _ { i } ) - w ( s _ { i + 1 } ) ) + f ( S ) w ( s _ { n } ) } \\ & { = \displaystyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } w ( s _ { i } ) ( f ( U _ { i } ) - f ( U _ { i - 1 } ) ) = \displaystyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } w ( s _ { i } ) x ( s _ { i } ) = w ^ { \mathsf { T } } x . } \end{array}
$$

This also gives a dual solution to the corresponding LP-formulation of the problem.

Maximization over intersections. Let $\zeta _ { 1 }$ and $\zeta _ { 2 }$ be lattice families of subsets of $S$ and let $f _ { 1 }$ and $f _ { 2 }$ be submodular functions on $\zeta _ { 1 }$ and $\zeta _ { 2 }$ respectively. Let $c _ { i }$ be specified by $L _ { i }$ , $M _ { i }$ , and $\preceq _ { i }$ .

Find a number $\alpha > 0$ satisfying (49.20) for both $f = f _ { 1 }$ and $f = f _ { 2 }$ . So by (49.21), $\alpha | S | + \operatorname* { m a x } _ { i = 1 , 2 } | f _ { i } ( L _ { i } ) |$ is an upper bound on $| f _ { i } ( U ) |$ for each $i \in \{ 1 , 2 \}$ and each $U \in { \mathcal { C } } _ { i }$ . Define

$$
K : = | S | ( \alpha | S | + \operatorname* { m a x } _ { i = 1 , 2 } | f _ { i } ( L _ { i } ) | ) .
$$

Now for $i = 1 , 2$ and $U \subseteq S$ , let $f _ { i } ( U ) : = f _ { i } ( \overline { { U } } ) + K | \overline { { U } } \triangle U |$ (where $\overline { U }$ is taken with respect to $\mathcal { C } _ { i }$ ). So $\bar { f } _ { 1 }$ and $f _ { 2 }$ are submodular (by Theorem 49.2). Then:

$$
\operatorname* { m a x } \{ w ^ { \mathsf { T } } x \mid x \in E P _ { f _ { 1 } } \cap E P _ { f _ { 2 } } \} = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ w ^ { \mathsf { T } } x \mid x \in E P _ { \bar { f } _ { 1 } } \cap E P _ { \bar { f } _ { 2 } } \} ,
$$

if the first maximum is finite. Clearly $\geq$ holds in (49.29), since $E P _ { \bar { f } _ { i } } \subseteq E P _ { f _ { i } }$ for $i = 1 , 2$ . To see equality, each face of $E P _ { f _ { 1 } } \cap E P _ { f _ { 2 } }$ is determined by equations $x ( U ) = f _ { i } ( U )$ for $i = 1 , 2$ and $U \in { \mathcal { D } } _ { i }$ , where $\mathcal { D } _ { i }$ is a chain of sets in $c _ { i }$ . So it is determined by a system of linear equations with totally unimodular constraint set and right-hand sides determined by function values of $f _ { 1 }$ and $f _ { 2 }$ . So each face contains a vector $x$ with $| x _ { s } | \le K$ for all $s \in S$ (by (49.28), since the inverse of a nonsingular totally unimodular matrix has all its entries in $\{ 0 , \pm 1 \}$ ). But any such $x$ belongs to $E P _ { \bar { f } _ { 1 } } \cap E P _ { \bar { f } _ { 2 } }$ , since for $i = 1 , 2$ and $U \subseteq S$ , we have:

$$
x ( U ) \leq x ( \overline { { U } } ) + K | \overline { { U } } \triangle U | \leq f _ { i } ( \overline { { U } } ) + K | \overline { { U } } \triangle U | = \bar { f } _ { i } ( U )
$$

(where $\overline { U }$ is taken with respect to $\mathit { \Delta } _ { \mathit { c } _ { i } }$ ). So we have (49.29).

Therefore, by Corollary 47.4d, we can maximize $w ^ { 1 } x$ over $E P _ { f _ { 1 } } \cap E P _ { f _ { 2 } }$ in strongly polynomial time. Note that for any $w \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { S }$ , we can decide in strongly polynomial time if the first maximum in (49.29) is finite. For this, we should decide if there exist $w _ { 1 } , w _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { Q } _ { + } ^ { S }$ such that $w = w _ { 1 } + w _ { 2 }$ and such that for $i = 1 , 2$ : $w _ { i } ( s ) = 0$ for $s \in S \setminus L _ { i }$ and $u \preceq i \ v$ implies $w _ { i } ( u ) \geq w _ { i } ( v )$ for all $u , v$ . This can be reduced to checking if a certain digraph with lengths has no negative-length directed circuit.

# 49.4. Submodular functions on an intersecting family

We next consider functions defined on a broader class of collections, the intersecting families, where the function satisfies a restricted form of submodularity. It yields an extension of the Dilworth truncation studied in Chapter 48.

A family $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ of sets is called an intersecting family if for all $T , U \in { \mathcal { C } }$ one has:

$$
{ \mathrm { i f ~ } } T \cap U \neq \emptyset { \mathrm { , ~ t h e n ~ } } T \cap U , T \cup U \in { \mathcal { C } }
$$

Let $c$ be an intersecting family. A function $f : C \to \mathbb { R }$ is called submodular on intersecting pairs, or intersecting submodular, if

$$
f ( T ) + f ( U ) \geq f ( T \cap U ) + f ( T \cup U )
$$

for all $T , U \in { \mathcal { C } }$ with $T \cap U \neq \emptyset$ .

Consider the system

$$
x ( U ) \leq f ( U ) { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } } U \in { \mathcal { C } } ,
$$

and the problem dual to maximizing $w ^ { 1 } x$ over (49.33), for $w \in \mathbb { R } ^ { S }$ :

$$
\operatorname* { m i n } \{ \sum _ { U \in { \mathcal C } } y ( U ) f ( U ) \mid y \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { \mathcal C } , \sum _ { U \in { \mathcal C } } y ( U ) \chi ^ { U } = w \} .
$$

Recall that a collection $\mathcal { F }$ of sets is called laminar if

T ∩ U = ∅ or $T \subseteq U$ or $U \subseteq T$ , for all $T , U \in { \mathcal { F } }$ .

A basic result (proved with a method due to Edmonds [1970b]) is:

Theorem 49.3. Let $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ be an intersecting family of subsets of a set $S$ , let $f : C \to \mathbb { R }$ be intersecting submodular and let $w \in \mathbb { R } ^ { S }$ . Then (49.34) has an optimum solution $y$ with ${ \mathcal { F } } : = \{ U \in { \mathcal { C } } \mid y ( U ) > 0 \}$ laminar.

Proof. Let $y : C \to \mathbb { R } _ { + }$ achieve this minimum, with

$$
\sum _ { U \in { \mathcal { C } } } y ( U ) | U | | S \setminus U |
$$

as small as possible. Assume that $\mathcal { F }$ is not laminar, and choose $T , U \in { \mathcal { F } }$ violating (49.35). Let $\alpha : = \operatorname* { m i n } \{ y ( T ) , y ( U ) \}$ . Decrease $y ( T )$ and $y ( U )$ by $\alpha$ , and increase $y ( T \cap U )$ and $y ( T \cup U )$ by $\alpha$ . Since

$$
\chi ^ { T \cap U } + \chi ^ { T \cup U } = \chi ^ { T } + \chi ^ { U } ,
$$

$y$ remains a feasible solution of (49.34). As moreover

$$
f ( T \cap U ) + f ( T \cup U ) \leq f ( T ) + f ( U ) ,
$$

$f$ remains optimum. However, by Theorem 2.1, sum (49.36) decreases, contradicting our assumption.

It gives the box-total dual integrality of (49.33):

Corollary 49.3a. Let $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ be an intersecting family of subsets of a set $S$ and let $f : C \to \mathbb { R }$ be intersecting submodular. Then system (49.33) is box-TDI.

Proof. Consider problem (49.34) dual to maximizing $w ^ { 1 } x$ over (49.33). By Theorem 49.3, this minimum is attained by a $y$ with ${ \mathcal { F } } : = \{ U \in { \mathcal { C } } \mid y ( U ) > 0 \}$ laminar. As the matrix of constraints corresponding to $\mathcal { F }$ is totally unimodular (Theorem 41.11), Theorem 5.35 gives the corollary. I

# 49.5. Intersection

Again, these results can be extended in a natural way to pairs of functions, by derivation from Theorem 49.3.

Corollary 49.3b. For $i = 1 , 2$ , let $\mathcal { C } _ { i }$ be an intersecting family of subsets of a set $S$ and let $f _ { i } : { \mathcal { C } } _ { i }  \mathbb { R }$ be intersecting submodular. Then the system

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { x ( U ) \leq f _ { 1 } ( U ) \ f o r \ U \in \mathcal { C } _ { 1 } , } \\ & { x ( U ) \leq f _ { 2 } ( U ) \ f o r \ U \in \mathcal { C } _ { 2 } , } \end{array}
$$

is box-TDI.

Proof. Choose $w \in \mathbb { R } ^ { S }$ , and consider the problem dual to maximizing $w ^ { 1 } x$ over (49.39):

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \operatorname* { m i n } \{ \displaystyle \sum _ { U \in \mathcal { C } _ { 1 } } y _ { 1 } ( U ) f _ { 1 } ( U ) + \displaystyle \sum _ { U \in \mathcal { C } _ { 2 } } y _ { 2 } ( U ) f _ { 2 } ( U ) \mid } \\ & { \qquad y _ { 1 } \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { \mathcal { C } _ { 1 } } , y _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { \mathcal { C } _ { 2 } } , \displaystyle \sum _ { U \in \mathcal { C } _ { 1 } } y _ { 1 } ( U ) \chi ^ { U } + \displaystyle \sum _ { U \in \mathcal { C } _ { 2 } } y _ { 2 } ( U ) \chi ^ { U } = w \} . } \end{array}
$$

Let $y _ { 1 } , y _ { 2 }$ attain the minimum. For $i \in \{ 1 , 2 \}$ , define

$$
w _ { i } : = \sum _ { U \in \mathcal { C } _ { i } } y _ { i } ( U ) \chi ^ { U } .
$$

By Theorem 49.3,

$$
\operatorname* { m i n } \{ \sum _ { U \in \mathcal { C } _ { i } } y _ { i } ( U ) f _ { i } ( U ) \mid y _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { \mathcal { C } _ { i } } , \sum _ { U \in \mathcal { C } _ { i } } y _ { i } ( U ) \chi ^ { U } = w _ { i } \}
$$

has an optimum solution $y _ { i }$ with ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { i } : = \{ U \in { \mathcal { C } } _ { i } \mid y _ { i } ( U ) > 0 \}$ laminar.

As $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \cup \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ determine a totally unimodular matrix (by Theorem 41.11), Theorem 5.35 implies that system (49.39) is box-TDI.

This implies the integrality of polyhedra:

Corollary 49.3c. If $f _ { 1 }$ and $f _ { 2 }$ are integer, then $E P _ { f _ { 1 } } \cap E P _ { f _ { 2 } }$ is box-integer.

Proof. Directly from Corollary 49.3b.

# 49.6. From an intersecting family to a lattice family

Let $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ be an intersecting family of subsets of a set $S$ and let $f : C \to \mathbb { R }$ b e submodular on intersecting pairs. Let $\dot { \mathcal { C } }$ be the collection of all unions of sets in $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ . Since $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ is closed under unions of intersecting sets, $\check { \mathcal { C } }$ is equal to the collection of disjoint unions of nonempty sets in $c$ . It is not difficult to show that $\check { \mathcal { C } }$ is a lattice family and that $\varnothing \in { \check { \mathcal { C } } }$ .

Call a partition proper if its classes are nonempty. Define $\check { f } : \check { \mathcal { C } }  \mathbb { R }$ by:

$$
\check { f } ( U ) : = \operatorname* { m i n } \{ \sum _ { P \in \mathcal { P } } f ( P ) \mid \mathcal { P } \subseteq \mathcal { C } { \mathrm { ~ i s ~ a ~ p r o p e r ~ p a r t i t i o n ~ o f ~ } } U \} .
$$

for $U \in \check { \mathcal { C } }$ . So ${ \check { f } } ( \varnothing ) = 0$ . Then (Dunstan [1976]):

Theorem 49.4. $\check { f }$ is submodular.

Proof. Choose $T , U \in { \check { \mathcal { C } } }$ , and let $\mathcal { P }$ and $\mathcal { Q }$ be partitions of $T$ and $U$ (respectively) into nonempty sets in $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ with

$$
\breve { f } ( T ) = \sum _ { P \in \mathcal { P } } f ( P ) \ \mathrm { a n d } \ \breve { f } ( U ) = \sum _ { Q \in \mathcal { Q } } f ( Q ) .
$$

Consider the family $\mathcal { F }$ made by the union of $\mathcal { P }$ and $\mathcal { Q }$ (taking a set twice if it occurs in both partitions). We can transform $\mathcal { F }$ iteratively into a laminar family, by replacing any $X , Y \in { \mathcal { F } }$ with $X \cap Y \neq \emptyset$ and $X \ \subset \ Y \ \subset \ X$ by $X \cap Y , X \cup Y$ . In each iteration, the sum

$$
\sum _ { Z \in { \mathcal { F } } } f ( Z )
$$

does not increase (as $f$ is submodular on intersecting pairs). As at each iteration the sum

$$
\sum _ { Z \in { \mathcal { F } } } | Z | | S \setminus Z |
$$

decreases (by Theorem 2.1), this process terminates. We end up with a laminar family $\mathcal { F }$ .

The inclusionwise maximal sets in $\mathcal { F }$ form a partition $\mathcal { R }$ of $T \cup U$ , and the remaining sets form a partition $\boldsymbol { S }$ of $T \cap U$ . Therefore,

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \check { f } ( T \cup U ) + \check { f } ( T \cap U ) \le \displaystyle \sum _ { X \in { \mathcal R } } f ( X ) + \sum _ { Y \in { \mathcal S } } f ( Y ) } \\ & { \le \displaystyle \sum _ { P \in { \mathcal P } } f ( P ) + \sum _ { Q \in { \mathcal Q } } f ( Q ) = \check { f } ( T ) + \check { f } ( U ) , } \end{array}
$$

showing that $\check { f }$ is submodular.

Trivially, if $\varnothing \notin { \mathcal { C } }$ or if $f ( \varnothing ) \geq 0$ , then $E P _ { \check { f } } = E P _ { f }$ . Hence, by (49.9),

$$
\check { f } ( U ) = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ x ( U ) \mid U \in E P _ { f } \} .
$$

As we shall see in Section 49.7, this enables us to calculate $\dot { f }$ from a value giving oracle, using the greedy algorithm.

# 49.7. Complexity

The results of the previous section enable us to reduce algorithmic problems on intersecting submodular functions, to those on submodular functions on lattice families.

If $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ is an intersecting family on $S$ , then for each $s \in S$ , the collection $\mathcal { C } _ { s } : = \{ U \in \mathcal { C } \ | \ s \in U \}$ is a lattice family. So (like in Section 49.3) we can assume that $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ is given by a representation of $\mathit { \Delta } { \mathit { C } } _ { s }$ for each $s \in S$ , in terms of the pre-order $\preceq _ { s }$ given by: $u \preceq s \ v$ if and only if each set in $c$ containing $s$ and $v$ also contains $u$ , and by $M _ { s } : = \lceil \rceil \mathcal { C } _ { s }$ and $L _ { s } : = \cup \mathcal { C } _ { s }$ ; next to that we should know if $\emptyset$ belongs to $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ .

We can derive the information on $\check { \mathcal { C } }$ as follows:

$$
\cap { \check { \mathcal { C } } } = \emptyset , \bigcup { \check { \mathcal { C } } } = \bigcup _ { s \in S } L _ { s } ; u \preccurlyeq v { \mathrm { ~ i f ~ a n d ~ o n l y ~ i f ~ } } u \in M _ { v } .
$$

So we can decide in polynomial time if a set $U$ belongs to $\check { \mathcal { C } }$ .

For any intersecting submodular function $f$ on $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ , the restriction $f _ { s }$ of $f$ to $\mathit { \Delta } \mathit { \mathcal { C } } _ { s }$ is submodular. So by the results of Section 49.3, we can find a set minimizing $f$ in strongly polynomial time.

For any $U \in { \dot { \mathcal { C } } }$ , we can calculate $\check { f } ( U )$ , as defined in (49.43), in strongly polynomial time, having a value giving oracle for $f$ . To see this, we use (49.48). We can assume that $\varnothing \notin { \mathcal { C } }$ .

Order the elements of $U$ as $t _ { 1 } , \ldots , t _ { k }$ such that if $L _ { t _ { j } } \subset L _ { t _ { i } }$ , then $j < i$ . For $i = 0 , \ldots , k$ , let $U _ { i } : = L _ { t _ { 1 } } \cup \cdot \cdot \cdot \cup L _ { t _ { i } }$ . So $U _ { k } = U$ .

Initially, set $x ( t ) : = 0$ for each $t \in U$ . Next, for $i = 1 , \ldots , k$ , calculate

$$
\mu : = \operatorname* { m i n } \{ f ( T ) - x ( T ) \mid T \in \mathcal { C } , t _ { i } \in T \subseteq U _ { i } { \mathrm { , } } \quad
$$

and reset $x ( t _ { i } ) : = x ( t _ { i } ) + \mu$ . We prove, by induction on $i$ , that for $i = 0 , 1 , \ldots , k$ we have, after processing $t _ { 1 } , \ldots , t _ { i }$ :

(i) $x ( T ) \leq f ( T )$ for each $T \in { \mathcal { C } }$ with $T \subseteq U _ { i }$ ,   
(ii) for each $j = 1 , \dotsc , i$ there exists a $T \in { \mathcal { C } }$ with $t _ { j } \in T \subseteq U _ { i }$ and $x ( T ) = f ( T )$ .

For $i = 0$ this is trivial. Let $i \geq 1$ . Consider any $T \in { \mathcal { C } }$ with $T \subseteq U _ { i }$ . If $t _ { i } \in T$ , then $x ( T ) \leq f ( T )$ , as at processing $t _ { i }$ we have added $\mu$ to $x ( t _ { i } )$ . If $t _ { i } \notin T$ , then $T \subseteq U _ { i - 1 }$ . For suppose that there exists a $t _ { j } \in T$ with $t _ { j } \notin U _ { i - 1 }$ . So $j > i$ and $t _ { j } \in L _ { t _ { i } }$ , and therefore $L _ { t _ { j } } \subseteq L _ { t _ { i } }$ , implying $L _ { t _ { j } } ~ = ~ L _ { t _ { i } }$ (since if $L _ { t _ { j } } \subset L _ { t _ { i } }$ , then $j < i$ ). But then $t _ { i } \in L _ { t _ { j } } \subseteq T$ , contradicting the fact that $t _ { i } \notin T$ . So $T \subseteq U _ { i - 1 }$ . As $t _ { i } \notin T$ , $x ( T )$ did not change at processing $t _ { i }$ , and hence we know $x ( T ) \leq f ( T )$ by induction. This proves (49.51)(i).

To see (49.51)(ii), choose $j \le i$ . If $j = i$ , there exists after processing $t _ { i }$ a $T$ as required, as we have added $\mu$ to $x ( t _ { i } )$ . If $j < i$ , by induction there exists a $T \in { \mathcal { C } }$ with $t _ { j } \in T \subseteq U _ { i - 1 }$ and $x ( T ) = f ( T )$ before processing $t _ { i }$ . If $t _ { i } \notin T$ , $x ( T ) = f ( T )$ is maintained at processing $t _ { i }$ . If $t _ { i } \in T$ , then $t _ { i } \in U _ { i - 1 }$ , and so $t _ { i } \in L _ { t _ { j } }$ for some $j < i$ . Hence $L _ { t _ { i } } \subseteq L _ { t _ { j } }$ . So, by the choice of the order of $U$ , $L _ { t _ { i } } = L _ { t _ { j } }$ . Hence before processing $t _ { i }$ we have $x ( T ^ { \prime } ) \leq f ( T ^ { \prime } )$ for each $T ^ { \prime } \subseteq U _ { i }$ . So, as $x ( T ) = f ( T )$ and $t _ { i } \in T$ , $x ( t _ { i } )$ is not modified at processing $t _ { i }$ . Therefore, $x ( T ) = f ( T )$ holds also after processing $t _ { i }$ . This proves (49.51)(ii).

This shows (49.51), which gives, taking $i = k$ , that $x ( T ) \leq f ( T )$ for each $T \in { \mathcal { C } }$ with $T \subseteq U$ , and that for each $t \in U$ , we have a $T$ containing $t$ with $x ( T ) = f ( T )$ . We can replace any two $T$ and $T ^ { \prime }$ with $T \cap T ^ { \prime } \neq \emptyset$ by $T \cup T ^ { \prime }$ . We end up with a partition $\tau$ of $U$ with $\begin{array} { r } { x ( U ) = \sum _ { T \in \mathcal { T } } f ( T ) } \end{array}$ . Hence we know

$$
\check { f } ( U ) \geq x ( U ) = \sum _ { T \in { \mathcal { T } } } x ( T ) = \sum _ { T \in { \mathcal { T } } } f ( T ) \geq \check { f } ( U ) ,
$$

and therefore we have equality throughout.

Having this, we can reduce the problem of maximizing $w ^ { 1 } x$ over $E P _ { f }$ , where $f$ is intersecting submodular, to that of maximizing $w ^ { 1 } x$ over $E P _ { \check { f } }$ ,

which can be done in strongly polynomial time by the results of Section 49.3.   
Similarly for intersections of two such polyhedra $E P _ { f _ { 1 } }$ and $E P _ { f _ { 2 } }$ .

# 49.8. Intersecting a polymatroid and a contrapolymatroid

For an intersecting family $c$ , a function $g : { \mathcal { C } }  \mathbb { R }$ is called supermodular on intersecting pairs, or intersecting supermodular, if $- g$ is intersecting submodular.

Let $S$ be a finite set. Let $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ and $\mathcal { D }$ be collections of subsets of $S$ and let $f : C \to \mathbb { R }$ and $g : \mathcal { D }  \mathbb { R }$ . Consider the system

$$
\begin{array} { r l } { x ( U ) \leq f ( U ) } & { { } { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } } U \in { \mathcal { C } } , } \\ { x ( U ) \geq g ( U ) } & { { } { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } } U \in { \mathcal { D } } . } \end{array}
$$

Theorem 49.5. If $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ and $\mathcal { D }$ are intersecting families, $f : { \mathcal { C } }  \mathbb { R }$ is intersecting submodular, and $g : \mathcal { D }  \mathbb { R }$ is intersecting supermodular, then system (49.53) is box-TDI.

Proof. Choose $w \in \mathbb { Z } ^ { S }$ , and consider the dual problem of maximizing $w ^ { 1 } x$ over (49.53):

$$
\begin{array} { r l } { \operatorname* { m i n } \{ \underset { U \in \mathcal { C } } { \sum } y ( U ) f ( U ) - \underset { U \in \mathcal { D } } { \sum } z ( U ) g ( U ) \mid } & { } \\ { y \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { \mathcal { C } } , z \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { \mathcal { D } } , \underset { U \in \mathcal { C } } { \sum } y ( U ) \chi ^ { U } - \underset { U \in \mathcal { D } } { \sum } z ( U ) \chi ^ { U } = w \} . } \end{array}
$$

Let $y , z$ attain this minimum. Define

$$
u : = \sum _ { U \in { \mathcal C } } y ( U ) \chi ^ { U } { \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } } v : = \sum _ { U \in { \mathcal D } } z ( U ) \chi ^ { U } .
$$

So $y$ attains

$$
\operatorname* { m i n } \{ \sum _ { U \in { \mathcal { C } } } y ( U ) f ( U ) \mid y \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { c } , \sum _ { U \in { \mathcal { C } } } y ( U ) \chi ^ { U } = u \}
$$

and $z$ attains

$$
\operatorname* { m a x } \{ \sum _ { U \in \mathcal { D } } z ( U ) g ( U ) \mid z \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { \mathcal { D } } , \sum _ { U \in \mathcal { D } } z ( U ) \chi ^ { U } = v \} .
$$

By Theorem 49.3, (49.56) has an optimum solution $y$ with ${ \mathcal { F } } : = \{ U \in { \mathcal { C } } \mid$ $y ( U ) > 0 \}$ laminar. Similarly, (49.57) has an optimum solution $z$ with $\mathcal { G } : =$ $\{ U \in { \mathcal { D } } \mid z ( U ) > 0 \}$ laminar. Now $\mathcal { F }$ and $\mathcal { G }$ determine a totally unimodular submatrix (by Theorem 41.11), and hence by Theorem 5.35, (49.53) is boxTDI. I

# 49.9. Submodular functions on a crossing family

Finally, we consider submodular functions defined on a crossing family. The results discussed above for submodular functions on intersecting families do not all transfer to crossing families. But certain restricted versions still hold.

A family $c$ of subsets of a set $S$ is called a crossing family if for all $T , U \in { \mathcal { C } }$ one has:

$$
{ \mathrm { i f ~ } } T \cap U \neq \emptyset { \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } } T \cup U \neq S { \mathrm { , ~ t h e n ~ } } T \cap U , T \cup U \in { \mathcal { C } } .
$$

A function $f : C \to \mathbb { R }$ , defined on a crossing family $c$ , is called submodular on crossing pairs, or crossing submodular, if for all $T , U \in { \mathcal { C } }$ with $T \cap U \neq \emptyset$ and $T \cup U \neq S$ :

$$
f ( T ) + f ( U ) \geq f ( T \cap U ) + f ( T \cup U ) .
$$

In general, the system

$$
x ( U ) \leq f ( U ) { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } } U \in { \mathcal { C } }
$$

is not TDI. For instance, if $S = \{ 1 , 2 , 3 \}$ , $\mathcal { C } = \{ \{ 1 , 2 \} , \{ 1 , 3 \} , \{ 2 , 3 \} \}$ , from $S$ , and $f ( U ) : = 1$ for each $U \in { \mathcal { C } }$ , then (49.60) not even determines an integer polyhedron (as $\left( { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } , { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } , { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \right) ^ { \mathsf { T } }$ is a vertex of it).

However, for any $k \in \mathbb R$ , the system

$$
\begin{array} { l } { x ( U ) \leq f ( U ) \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } U \in \mathcal { C } , } \\ { x ( S ) = k } \end{array}
$$

is box-TDI. This can be done by reduction to Corollary 49.3a. Similarly for pairs of such functions. This was shown by Frank [1982b,1984a] and Fujishige [1984e].

Let $c$ be a crossing family of subsets of a set $S$ . Let $\hat { \mathcal { C } }$ be the collection of all nonempty intersections of sets in $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ (we allow the intersection of 0 sets, so $S \in { \hat { \mathcal { C } } }$ ). Since $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ is a crossing family, we know

where a copartition of $U$ is a collection $\mathcal { P }$ of subsets of $S$ such that the collection $\{ S \setminus T \mid T \in { \mathcal { P } } \}$ is a partition of $U$ . We call the copartition proper if $T \neq S$ for each $T \in { \mathcal { P } }$ .

Note that, in (49.62), restricting $\mathcal { P }$ to proper copartitions of $S \setminus U$ , does not modify $\hat { \mathcal { C } }$ . We allow $\mathcal { P } = \emptyset$ , so $S \in { \hat { \mathcal { C } } }$ .

Define $\hat { f } : \mathcal { \hat { C } } \to \mathbb { R }$ by:

$$
{ \hat { f } } ( U ) : = \operatorname* { m i n } \{ \sum _ { P \in { \mathcal { P } } } f ( P ) \mid { \mathcal { P } } \subseteq { \mathcal { C } } { \mathrm { ~ i s ~ a ~ p r o p e r ~ c o p a r t i t i o n ~ o f ~ } } S \setminus U \}
$$

for $U \in { \hat { \mathcal { C } } }$ . So ${ \hat { f } } ( S ) = 0$ . Then:

Theorem 49.6. $\hat { \mathcal { C } }$ is an intersecting family and $\hat { f }$ is submodular on intersecting pairs.

Proof. Define, for $s \in S$ ,

$$
\hat { \mathcal { C } } _ { s } : = \{ U \in \hat { \mathcal { C } } \mid s \in U \} \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } \mathcal { D } : = \{ S \setminus U \mid s \in U \in \mathcal { C } \}
$$

As $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ is crossing, $\mathcal { D }$ is intersecting. Hence $\dot { \mathcal { D } }$ is a lattice family. As $\hat { \mathcal { C } } _ { s } ~ =$ $\{ S \setminus U \mid U \in { \tilde { \mathcal { D } } } \}$ , also $\hat { \mathcal { C } } _ { s }$ is a lattice family. As this is true for each $s \in S$ , $\hat { \mathcal { C } }$ is intersecting.

To prove that $\hat { f }$ is intersecting submodular, it suffices to show that for each $s \in S$ , the restriction $\hat { f } _ { s }$ of $\hat { f }$ to $\hat { \mathcal { C } } _ { s }$ is submodular. Define $g : \mathcal { D }  \mathbb { R }$ by $g ( U ) : = f ( S \setminus U )$ for $U \in \mathcal { D }$ . Then $g$ is intersecting submodular (as $f$ is crossing submodular). Hence, by Theorem 49.4, $\dot { g }$ is submodular on $\dot { \mathcal { D } }$ . As $\hat { f } _ { s } ( U ) = \check { g } ( S \backslash U )$ for $U \in \hat { \mathcal { C } } _ { s }$ , $\hat { f } _ { s }$ is submodular. I

Fujishige [1984e] showed that the following box-TDI result can be derived from Corollary 49.3a:

Theorem 49.7. Let $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ be a crossing family of subsets of $S$ , let $f : { \mathcal { C } }  \mathbb { R }$ be crossing submodular, and let $k \in \mathbb R$ . Then system (49.61) is box-TDI and determines the polyhedron of maximal vectors of $E P _ { f ^ { \prime } }$ for some submodular function $f ^ { \prime }$ defined on a lattice family.

Proof. We can assume that $k = 0$ , since, choosing any $t \in S$ and resetting $f ( U ) : = f ( U ) - k$ for all $U \in { \mathcal { C } }$ with $t \in U$ , does not change the box-total dual integrality of (49.61). We can also assume that $\varnothing \notin { \mathcal { C } }$ .

The box-total dual integrality of (49.61) follows from that of

$$
\begin{array} { l l } { x ( U ) \leq { \hat { f } } ( U ) \quad { \mathrm { f o r ~ } } U \in { \hat { \mathcal { C } } } , } \\ { x ( S ) = 0 , } \end{array}
$$

as (49.65) and (49.61) have the same solution set, and as each constraint in (49.65) is a nonnegative integer combination of constraints in (49.61). The box-total dual integrality of (49.65) follows from Corollary 49.3a (using Theorem 5.25). It also shows that the solution set of (49.61) is the set of maximal vectors of $E P _ { f ^ { \prime } }$ for some submodular function $f ^ { \prime }$ defined on a lattice family.

Frank and Tardos [1984b] observed that this implies a relation with matroids:

Corollary 49.7a. If $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ is a crossing family of subsets of a set $S$ , $f : C \to \mathbb { Z }$ is crossing submodular, and $k \in \mathbb { Z }$ , then the collection

$$
\{ B \subseteq S \mid | B | = k , | B \cap U | \leq f ( U ) \ f o r \ e a c h \ U \in { \mathcal { C } } \}
$$

forms the collection of bases of a matroid (if nonempty).

Proof. Directly from Theorem 49.7, using the observations on (44.43) and (49.11). I

Similarly, the box-total dual integrality of pairs of such systems follows:

Theorem 49.8. For $i = 1 , 2$ , let $\mathcal { C } _ { i }$ be a crossing family of subsets of a set $S$ , let $f _ { i } : { \mathcal { C } } _ { i }  \mathbb { R }$ be crossing submodular, and let $k \in \mathbb R$ . Then the system

$$
\begin{array} { l } { x ( U ) \leq f _ { 1 } ( U ) \ f o r \ U \in \mathcal C _ { 1 } , } \\ { x ( U ) \leq f _ { 2 } ( U ) \ f o r \ U \in \mathcal C _ { 2 } , } \\ { x ( S ) = k , } \end{array}
$$

is box-TDI.

Proof. Similar to the proof of the previous theorem, by reduction to Corollary 49.3b.

This implies the integrality of polyhedra:

Corollary 49.8a. For $i = 1 , 2$ , let $\mathit { \Delta } _ { \mathit { \phi } _ { i } }$ be a crossing family of subsets of a set $S$ , let $f _ { i } : C _ { i } \to \mathbb { R }$ be crossing submodular, and let $k \in \mathbb R$ . If $f _ { 1 }$ , $f _ { 2 }$ , and $k$ are integer, system (49.67) determines a box-integer polyhedron.

Proof. Directly from Theorem 49.8.

# 49.10. Complexity

The reduction given in the proof of Theorem 49.6 also enables us to calculate ${ \hat { f } } ( U )$ from a value giving oracle for $f$ , similar to the proof in Section 49.7. We assume that $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ is given by descriptions of the lattice families $\mathcal { C } _ { s , t } : = \{ U \in$ ${ \mathcal { C } } \mid s \in U , t \not \in U \}$ as in Section 49.3.

Note that

$$
E P _ { \hat { f } } \cap \{ x \mid x ( S ) = 0 \} = E P _ { f } \cap \{ x \mid x ( S ) = 0 \} .
$$

This follows from the fact that if $x \in E P _ { f }$ and $x ( S ) = 0$ , then for any $U \in { \hat { \mathcal { C } } }$ and any proper copartition $\mathcal { P } = \{ U _ { 1 } , \ldots , U _ { p } \}$ of $S \setminus U$ with $f ( U ) =$ $\textstyle \sum _ { P \in { \mathcal { P } } } f ( P )$ , one has:

$$
x ( U ) = - x ( S \setminus U ) = - \sum _ { P \in \mathcal P } x ( S \setminus P ) = \sum _ { P \in \mathcal P } x ( P ) \le \sum _ { P \in \mathcal P } f ( P )
$$

Having this, the problem of maximizing $w ^ { 1 } x$ over $E P _ { f } \cap \{ x \mid x ( S ) = 0 \}$ , where $f$ is crossing submodular, is reduced to the problem of maximizing $w ^ { 1 } x$ over $E P _ { \hat { f } } \cap \{ x \mid x ( S ) = 0 \}$ . The latter problem can be solved in strongly polynomial time by the results of Section 49.7. Similar results hold for intersections of two such polyhedra:

Theorem 49.9. For crossing families $\mathcal { C } _ { 1 } , \mathcal { C } _ { 2 }$ of subsets of a set $S$ , crossing submodular functions $f _ { 1 } : { \mathcal { C } } _ { 1 } \to \mathbb { Q }$ and $f _ { 2 } : C _ { 2 } \to \mathbb { Q }$ , $k \in \mathbb { Q }$ , and $w \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { S }$ , one can find an $x \in E P _ { f _ { 1 } } \cap E P _ { f _ { 2 } }$ with $x ( S ) = k$ and maximizing $w ^ { 1 } x$ in strongly polynomial time.

Proof. From the above.

If $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ is a crossing family and $f : C \to \mathbb { Q }$ is crossing submodular, then we can find its minimum value in polynomial time, as, for each $s , t \in S$ , we can minimize $f$ over the lattice family $\{ U \in { \mathcal { C } } \mid s \in U , t \not \in U \}$ , and take the minimum of all these minima, and of the values in $\varnothing$ and $S$ (if in $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { C } }$ ).

Hence we can decide in polynomial time if a given vector $x \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { S }$ belongs to $E P _ { f }$ , by testing if the minimum value of the crossing submodular function $g : { \mathcal { C } }  \mathbb { Q }$ defined by

$$
g ( U ) : = f ( U ) - x ( U )
$$

for $U \in { \mathcal { C } }$ , is nonnegative.

# 49.10a. Nonemptiness of the base polyhedron

Let $c$ be a crossing family of subsets of a set $S$ and let $f : C \to \mathbb { R }$ be crossing submodular. We give a theorem of Fujishige [1984e] characterizing when $E P _ { f }$ contains a vector $x$ with $x ( S ) = 0$ . If $S \in { \mathcal { C } }$ and $f ( S ) = 0$ , then the set $E P _ { f } \cap \{ x \mid x ( S ) = 0 \}$ is called the base polyhedron of $f$ .

To give the characterization, again call a collection ${ \mathcal { P } } \subseteq { \mathcal { C } }$ a copartition of $S$ if the collection $\{ S \setminus U \mid U \in { \mathcal { P } } \}$ is a partition of $S$ .

Theorem 49.10. $E P _ { f }$ contains a vector $_ x$ satisfying $x ( S ) = 0$ if and only if

$$
\sum _ { U \in { \mathcal { P } } } f ( U ) \geq 0
$$

for each partition or copartition ${ \mathcal { P } } \subseteq { \mathcal { C } }$ of $S$ . If moreover $f$ is integer, there exists an integer such vector $_ x$ .

Proof. The condition is necessary, since if $x \in E P _ { f }$ satisfies $x ( S ) = 0$ and ${ \mathcal { P } } \subseteq C$ is a partition of $S$ , then

$$
\sum _ { U \in { \mathcal { P } } } f ( U ) \geq \sum _ { U \in { \mathcal { P } } } x ( U ) = x ( S ) = 0 .
$$

Similarly, if $\mathcal { P } \subseteq \mathcal { C }$ is a copartition of $S$ , then

$$
\sum _ { U \in { \mathcal { P } } } f ( U ) \geq \sum _ { U \in { \mathcal { P } } } x ( U ) = \sum _ { U \in { \mathcal { P } } } ( x ( S ) - x ( S \setminus U ) ) = | { \mathcal { P } } | x ( S ) - x ( S ) = 0 .
$$

To see sufficiency, let $\mathcal { D } : = \hat { \mathcal { C } }$ and $g : = { \hat { f } } $ (cf. (49.62)). By Theorem 49.6, $\mathcal { D }$ is an intersecting family and $g$ is intersecting submodular. Moreover, $S \in { \mathcal { D } }$ . (i) $\sum _ { T \in \mathcal { F } } ^ { \mathrm { a l l ~ e l e m e n t s ~ o } }$ f $S$ are contained in the same number of sets in $\mathcal { F }$ ;
